title: Adaptation: how living things fit their place, their hunters and their prey

summary.text: A plain tiger butterfly is bright orange and flies slowly in the open, yet most birds leave her alone. Why? In this lesson you will sort animals by their eyes, test which tree shape carries the least snow, and test when a copied warning colour keeps working, using paper prey and a hungry hunter.
summary.art: Two orange and black butterflies that look almost the same sitting on a milkweed plant, with a bulbul on a branch looking at them and not moving.

intro.hook: A tiger is bright orange with black stripes. Yet a spotted deer often fails to notice a tiger lying in the grass. How can such a bright animal hide?
intro.text: The answer is in the deer's eyes. We have three kinds of colour cells in our eyes, and a deer has two. To a deer, orange looks much like the green of grass. So the tiger's coat is fitted to the eyes of her prey, as well as to the forest. In this lesson you look at how plants and animals are fitted to heat, water and cold. Then you look at how hunters and the hunted are fitted to each other. You pour rava snow on paper trees. You also hunt paper prey, to find out when a false warning works.
intro.art: A tiger lying in tall dry grass and green bushes, and beside it the same scene as a deer sees it, with the tiger's coat a dull green that fades into the grass.

outcomes: I can say what an adaptation is, and sort adaptations into body, behaviour and the body's inner working.
I can explain how plants are adapted to dry, wet and cold places, with an Indian example of each.
I can explain how animals are adapted to hot, wet and cold places, and compare two answers to one problem.
I can list adaptations of predators and of prey, and say how each one answers the other.
I can explain four kinds of camouflage, and say why camouflage depends on the eyes of the watcher.
I can explain warning colours and mimicry, and say when copying a warning stops working.
I can run a fair test with paper trees or paper prey, and say what my results show.
I can explain why an animal is at risk when her place changes quickly, with an Indian example.

terms.meaning: An inherited feature that helps a living thing survive and have young in their place.
terms.example: A camel's wide feet are an adaptation to soft sand. A deodar's sloping branches are an adaptation to snow.
terms.art: A camel's wide foot spread on sand beside a deodar branch bending under snow.

terms.meaning: Everything around a living thing: the heat, the water, the ground and the other living things.
terms.example: A lotus's environment is a pond. It includes the mud, the water, the fish and the dragonflies.
terms.art: A lotus plant in a pond with labels pointing to the mud, the water, a fish and a dragonfly.

terms.meaning: An adaptation in the shape or covering of the body.
terms.example: A snow leopard's wide, furry paws and a cactus's spines are structural adaptations.
terms.art: A close view of a snow leopard's wide furry paw pressed on snow.

terms.meaning: An adaptation in what a living thing does.
terms.example: Spotted deer feed in a herd. A spiny-tailed lizard rests in her burrow in the heat of noon.
terms.art: A lizard looking out of a burrow in dry ground under a hot midday sun.

terms.meaning: An adaptation in how the body works on the inside.
terms.example: A camel's body can warm up by about 6 degrees Celsius in the day without harm, so she sweats less.
terms.art: A camel standing in the desert sun with a small thermometer drawing beside her showing a rising level.

terms.meaning: An animal who catches and eats other animals.
terms.example: A tiger, a house gecko, a barn owl and a dragonfly are all predators.
terms.art: A house gecko on a wall near a tube light, about to catch a moth.

terms.meaning: An animal who is caught and eaten by a predator.
terms.example: A moth is prey for a gecko. The gecko is prey for a cat.
terms.art: A cat on a floor looking up at a gecko on the wall, who is looking at a moth.

terms.meaning: Colours, patterns or shapes that make a living thing hard to notice.
terms.example: A nightjar on dry leaves and a crab spider on a yellow flower are both camouflaged.
terms.art: A brown mottled nightjar sitting on dry leaves, almost impossible to pick out.

terms.meaning: Bold stripes or patches that break up the outline of a body. The watcher's eye then does not see one whole shape.
terms.example: A tiger's black stripes cut her body into pieces that look like shadows between grass stems.
terms.art: A tiger half hidden in tall grass, with the stripes lining up with the dark gaps between the stems.

terms.meaning: Camouflage in which an animal looks like some other thing that hunters ignore.
terms.example: A stick insect looks like a twig. A young common mormon caterpillar looks like a bird dropping.
terms.art: A small shiny brown and white caterpillar on a curry leaf that looks exactly like a bird dropping.

terms.meaning: Bright colours and bold patterns that tell hunters an animal is bitter, poisonous or able to sting.
terms.example: The orange and black of a plain tiger butterfly, and the yellow and black of a wasp.
terms.art: A yellow and black paper wasp beside an orange and black butterfly.

terms.meaning: Both are harmful chemicals. A poison does harm when it is eaten or touched. A venom is put into the body by a bite or a sting.
terms.example: A plain tiger butterfly is poisonous to eat. A Russell's viper is venomous, because she injects venom with her fangs.
terms.art: Two small pictures: a bird spitting out an orange butterfly, and the open mouth of a viper showing two fangs.

terms.meaning: One kind of living thing looking like another kind, and gaining from the likeness.
terms.example: A hoverfly has no sting, but she is striped yellow and black like a wasp.
terms.art: A hoverfly and a wasp side by side on a flower, both striped yellow and black.

terms.meaning: The model is the animal with the real defence. The mimic is the animal who copies the model's look.
terms.example: The bitter common rose butterfly is the model. Some female common mormon butterflies are her mimics.
terms.art: Two black butterflies with red spots and a white patch, one with a red body labelled model and one with a black body labelled mimic.

terms.meaning: All that an animal can see without moving her head.
terms.example: A rabbit's eyes are on the sides of the head. Her field of view goes almost all the way round.
terms.art: A rabbit seen from above with a wide shaded area showing nearly a full circle of view.

terms.meaning: Two kinds of living things changing over many generations, each because of the other.
terms.example: Many moths have ears that hear the calls of hunting bats. Some bats now call very softly.
terms.art: A bat flying behind a moth at night, with small curved lines for sound between them.

terms.meaning: So few in number that the whole kind may die out.
terms.example: Only about 100 to 150 great Indian bustards are left in the wild.
terms.art: A tall great Indian bustard standing in dry grassland with power lines far behind.

explanations.concept: What an adaptation is, and its three kinds
explanations.definition: An adaptation is an inherited feature that helps a living thing survive in their place. It also helps them to have young there.
explanations.description: Adaptations come in three kinds. A structural adaptation is part of the body's shape or covering, such as a camel's wide feet. A behavioural adaptation is something the living thing does, such as a desert lizard resting in a burrow at noon. A physiological adaptation is a way the body works inside. A camel's body can warm up by about 6 degrees Celsius during the day without harm. So she sweats less and saves water. Most living things use all three kinds together. An adaptation is passed from parents to young. That makes it different from getting used to a place within one lifetime. An adaptation also helps only in the right place. Wide feet help a camel on sand and would slow her down on rocks.
examples: Structural: the hollow fangs of a Russell's viper.
Behavioural: spotted deer feed in a herd and look up often.
Physiological: a cactus opens the tiny holes in her skin only at night. The air is cool then, and less water escapes.
explanations.art: Three small pictures in a row: a camel's wide foot, a lizard in a burrow, and a cactus at night under the moon.

explanations.concept: Plants are adapted to dry, wet and cold places
explanations.definition: A plant stays in one spot for life. So the shape and working of their body must suit the heat, water and cold there.
explanations.description: In a hot, dry place, rain is rare and dries fast. A cactus has spines where other plants have leaves, so little water escapes. Her thick stem stores water under a waxy skin. Her roots are shallow and wide, and catch a short shower before it sinks away. The khejri tree of the Thar does the opposite, and sends one root many metres down to deep water. In a pond, a lotus has other problems. Her wide leaves float, and their waxy tops shed water. Her stems hold air tubes that carry oxygen down to roots in airless mud. In the mangrove forests of Pichavaram and the Sundarbans, the mud is soft and salty. Some mangrove trees stand on arching stilt roots. Others pass extra salt out through their leaves. In the rainy forests of the Western Ghats, many leaves end in a long, narrow drip tip. Rain runs to the tip and falls off, so the leaf dries sooner. A peepal leaf has such a tip. On cold Himalayan slopes, firs, spruces and young deodars grow as narrow cones. Their branches slope down and bend. In the Snow Load Test experiment in this lesson, a steep paper cone sheds almost all the rava snow poured on top. A flat paper circle keeps all of the rava. Real snow slides off a cone-shaped tree in the same way, before the weight can snap the branches. The needle leaves are thin and waxy, so they lose little water while the ground is frozen.
examples: Dry: a cactus with spines, a thick stem and a waxy skin.
Wet: a lotus with floating leaves and air tubes in her stems.
Salty mud: a mangrove tree on stilt roots at Pichavaram in Tamil Nadu.
Heavy rain: a peepal leaf with a long drip tip.
Snow: a deodar with sloping branches and needle leaves in Himachal Pradesh.
explanations.art: Five plants in a row, each in their own place: a cactus on sand, a lotus on a pond, a mangrove on stilt roots, a peepal leaf dripping rain, and a cone-shaped deodar in snow.

explanations.concept: Animals are adapted to hot, wet and cold places
explanations.definition: An animal's body, behaviour and inner working suit the place where their kind has lived for a very long time.
explanations.description: In the Thar desert the problems are heat, thirst and loose sand. A camel stores fat in her hump and can go a week or more without drinking. Long eyelashes and nostrils that close keep the sand out, and wide feet stop her sinking. In a wet place the problems are moving, breathing and feeding in water. A fish has fins to steer and gills that take in oxygen dissolved in the water. A duck has webbed feet, and oil on her feathers keeps them dry. A flamingo wades on long thin legs and strains tiny food from salty water with a bent beak. Seabirds drink sea water, and glands above their eyes pass the extra salt out. In the cold of Ladakh the problem is losing heat. A yak has a thick double coat. A snow leopard has thick fur, wide furry paws, and a long tail that she wraps around her face. One problem often has several answers. In desert heat, a camel lets her body warm up. A spiny-tailed lizard goes underground, and a desert fox loses heat through large ears. Putting these answers side by side shows what the problem really is. In a desert, it is staying alive in great heat with very little water.
examples: Hot and dry: the camel and the spiny-tailed lizard of the Thar.
Wet: flamingos at Pulicat Lake and in the Rann of Kutch.
Cold: the snow leopard and the yak of Ladakh.
explanations.art: Three scenes side by side: a camel on a dune, flamingos wading in a shallow lake, and a snow leopard on a snowy ledge with her tail curled round her.

explanations.concept: Predators are adapted to find, reach and kill prey
explanations.definition: A predator is an animal who catches and eats other animals. Those other animals are the prey.
explanations.description: A predator has three problems to solve, in order. The first is to find the prey. An eagle's eyes are far sharper than ours. A barn owl can catch a mouse in complete darkness by hearing alone. Most hunters have both eyes at the front of the face. Both eyes then see the same prey, and the brain uses the two views to judge distance. The second problem is to get within reach. A tiger uses camouflage and creeps close before a short rush. A cheetah uses speed, and can pass 90 kilometres an hour in a short dash. A spider builds a web and waits. Dholes, the wild dogs of Indian forests, hunt as a pack and tire out a deer. The third problem is to kill. Hunters have long pointed teeth, claws or talons, and some snakes inject venom. A few plants are predators too. The pitcher plant of Meghalaya traps insects in a cup of liquid and digests them. Many predators are also prey. A house gecko hunts moths, and a cat hunts the gecko.
examples: Finding: a barn owl hears a mouse under dry leaves.
Reaching: a tiger stalks to within a few leaps before she rushes.
Killing: a Russell's viper injects venom through hollow fangs.
Teamwork: a pack of dholes brings down a sambar deer.
explanations.art: A tiger's face seen from the front with both eyes looking straight ahead, and two faint lines from the eyes meeting at a deer in the distance.

explanations.concept: Prey are adapted to notice, escape and resist
explanations.definition: Prey animals have adaptations that help them notice a hunter early, avoid being found, get away, or fight back.
explanations.description: Each prey adaptation answers one of the predator's three problems. To notice a hunter early, a deer has eyes on the sides of her head. She sees almost all the way round, though she judges distance less well. Her large ears turn towards a sound. Spotted deer feed below langurs, who see far from the treetops and bark at a tiger. To avoid being found, many prey animals use camouflage and keep still. To get away, a blackbuck can run at up to about 80 kilometres an hour and swerves sharply. A house gecko drops her tail, and the wriggling tail holds the hunter's eye while she runs. An octopus squirts ink and jets away. To resist, a pangolin rolls into a ball of hard scales. A porcupine raises her quills, and bees sting together. Living in a group helps in two more ways. Each animal is one among many, so the chance that the hunter picks her is small. Animals in the middle are also shielded by those outside. In the Edge or Middle activity in this lesson, a rolling marble plays a tiger, and 19 chickpeas, called chana, play a herd of deer. The marble tiger nearly always touches a chana on the outer ring of the herd first. Plants are prey too. They resist with thorns, tough leaves and bitter chemicals.
examples: Noticing: a spotted deer's side-facing eyes and turning ears.
Escaping: a house gecko's tail that breaks off and wriggles.
Resisting: an Indian pangolin's ball of scales.
A plant resisting: the bitter leaves of a neem tree.
explanations.art: A herd of spotted deer feeding under a tree full of langurs, with one deer's head raised and her ears turned towards tall grass.

explanations.concept: Camouflage: four ways to go unnoticed
explanations.definition: Camouflage is any colour, pattern or shape that makes a living thing hard to notice or hard to recognise.
explanations.description: There are four main kinds. The first is matching the background, as a nightjar matches dry leaves. The second is a disruptive pattern. Bold stripes or patches break the body's outline into pieces, so the watcher does not see one animal shape. A tiger's stripes work this way among grass stems and shadows. The third is countershading. Many animals are dark on top and pale below. This cancels the shadow on the belly and makes the body look flat. The fourth is masquerade. The animal can be seen, but looks like something not worth eating. A stick insect looks like a twig. The Indian oakleaf butterfly looks like a dead leaf when her wings are closed. Hunters use camouflage as much as prey do. A crab spider on a yellow flower is yellow, and bees land within reach. Camouflage is always fitted to a particular eye. A tiger looks bright orange to us. A deer's eyes have two kinds of colour cells, and ours have three. To a deer, orange looks much like green. So the same coat is easy for us to see and hard for a deer to see.
examples: Matching: a green vine snake among green stems.
Disruptive pattern: the stripes of a tiger.
Countershading: a mackerel with a dark back and a silver belly.
Masquerade: a young common mormon caterpillar who looks like a bird dropping.
explanations.art: Four small panels: a nightjar on leaves, a tiger in grass, a fish dark above and pale below, and a butterfly that looks like a dead leaf on a twig.

explanations.concept: Warning colours: easy to see and easy to remember
explanations.definition: Warning colours are bright colours and bold patterns on an animal who is poisonous, bitter or able to sting.
explanations.description: Warning colours are the opposite of camouflage. The animal gains by being noticed. A plain tiger caterpillar eats milkweed, a plant with poison in the sap. She keeps the poison in her body for life. The butterfly is orange, black and white, and flies slowly in the open. A young bird who eats one is sick, or spits her out. The bird then avoids that pattern, often for a long time. Red, orange and yellow with black stand out against green leaves and brown ground. A bold pattern is also easy to remember, and that helps the bird as well as the butterfly. Wasps, blister beetles, ladybirds and the banded krait all carry warning colours. A cobra spreads her hood and a saw-scaled viper rubs her scales to make a rasping sound. These are warnings too. A warning works because hunters learn from a bad meal. That means the warning protects the kind of animal as a whole, and not every single one. A few of them are still tasted and die while the hunters are learning.
examples: A plain tiger butterfly on a milkweed plant by the road.
A yellow and black paper wasp at her nest under a window ledge.
A banded krait with wide yellow and black bands.
An orange and black blister beetle on a flower.
explanations.art: A young bulbul spitting out an orange butterfly, and in a second panel the same bird later turning away from another orange butterfly.

explanations.definition: Mimicry is one kind of living thing looking like another kind, and gaining from the likeness. The animal who is copied is called the model, and the copier is called the mimic.
explanations.description: In the first kind of mimicry, a harmless animal copies a harmful one. It is called Batesian mimicry, after Henry Walter Bates, who described it in 1862. The female danaid eggfly tastes fine, but she looks like the bitter plain tiger. A hoverfly has no sting, but she is striped like a wasp. Some female common mormon butterflies copy the bitter common rose. Birds who have learned to avoid the model leave the mimic alone as well. This works only while birds keep meeting the real, harmful kind. In the Copycat Test experiment in this lesson, a hunter usually stops eating striped squares when most of them are bitter. When most patterned squares are harmless, the hunter learns that the pattern is safe and eats them. So mimics are safest when they are fewer than their models. In the second kind of mimicry, two harmful kinds look alike. It is called Müllerian mimicry, after Fritz Müller. Many wasps and bees share yellow and black stripes. A bird then has only one pattern to learn, and fewer of each kind die while birds are learning. In the common mormon, only females are mimics. In 2014 Krushnamegh Kunte's team in Bengaluru found that a single gene, called doublesex, switches the copied pattern on.
examples: Model: the plain tiger. Mimic: the female danaid eggfly.
Model: the common rose. Mimic: one form of the female common mormon.
Model: a paper wasp. Mimic: a hoverfly.
Two harmful kinds that share stripes: a paper wasp and a rock bee.
explanations.art: Two pairs of look-alike butterflies, each pair with one labelled model and one labelled mimic, and a bird looking at both pairs.

explanations.concept: Hunters and hunted shape each other
explanations.definition: Co-evolution is two kinds of living things changing over many generations, each because of the other.
explanations.description: In every generation, some deer are a little quicker to notice a tiger. They are more likely to live and have fawns. The fawns inherit their parents' features. In the same forest, the tigers who stalk a little better eat more often and raise more cubs. Over thousands of generations, both kinds change. A deer's speed is partly the work of tigers, and a tiger's stealth is partly the work of deer. Scientists call this an arms race. In 2018 Alan Wilson's team put recording collars on lions, zebras, cheetahs and impalas in Botswana. The hunters were faster and stronger than their prey. The prey could still escape, by running a little slower and turning sharply at the last moment. Bats and moths are in the same kind of race. Many moths have ears that hear a bat's calls, and some bats have taken to calling very softly. Plants and their eaters shape each other too. Milkweed makes poison, and the plain tiger caterpillar eats milkweed all the same and uses the poison herself. How these changes build up is called natural selection, and a later unit explains it.
examples: Cheetah and blackbuck: speed against sharp turns.
Bat and moth: calls against ears.
Milkweed and plain tiger caterpillar: poison against a body that can store poison.
explanations.art: A cheetah at full stretch behind a blackbuck who is turning sharply, with dust flying from her hooves.

explanations.concept: When a place changes fast, an adaptation can stop fitting
explanations.definition: An adaptation fits the place where it arose. If the place changes quickly, the same feature may stop helping, or may even do harm.
explanations.description: The peppered moth of England is pale and speckled. On tree trunks covered with pale lichen, birds seldom found her. In the 1800s, smoke from factories killed the lichen and blackened the trunks around Manchester. Pale moths now stood out, and birds ate them. A rare dark form was hard to see on the dark bark. By 1895 almost all the moths near Manchester were dark. When the air was cleaned after 1956, pale moths became common again. Bodies can follow a change in this way only if it is slow enough, and only over many generations. The great Indian bustard is a large bird of dry grassland. Like many prey birds, she has eyes on the sides of her head. She watches the ground and the sky for foxes and eagles. She sees poorly straight ahead while flying. That did no harm for thousands of years. Now power lines cross her grassland, and bustards fly into the wires and die. Only about 100 to 150 are left. Vultures can eat rotting meat safely. But a cattle medicine called diclofenac poisoned them. India lost more than 95 of every 100 vultures before the medicine was banned for cattle in 2006.
examples: The peppered moth: pale wings stopped hiding her on sooty bark.
The great Indian bustard: side-facing eyes do not show her the power lines ahead.
Indian vultures: a strong stomach was no defence against a new medicine.
explanations.art: A great Indian bustard flying low over dry grassland towards thin power lines, with shining flaps hung on one of the wires.

explanations.concept: Why does a zebra have stripes?
explanations.definition: Scientists do not yet agree on what a zebra's stripes are for.
explanations.description: Not every adaptation has an agreed explanation. A zebra's stripes are bold and easy to see on an open plain. Scientists have argued about them for 150 years. The question is still open, though one answer now has the strongest evidence. It is a reminder to test an explanation, however sensible it sounds.
examples: A zebra standing in short grass is easy for a person to see from far away.
Biting flies land less often on striped surfaces than on plain ones.

perspectives.explanation: The stripes keep biting flies away. In 2019 the team dressed horses in striped coats. Flies came near, but few managed to land on the stripes.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study heat, such as Alison Cobb and Stephen Cobb
perspectives.explanation: Black stripes warm up more than white ones in the sun. This may stir small currents of air over the skin and help a zebra to cool.

perspectives.who: An older view, held since the 1800s
perspectives.explanation: The stripes are camouflage, or they dazzle a lion when a herd runs. Tests have found little support for this, because lions see the stripes only when they are already very close.

explanations.art: A zebra standing beside a brown horse, with small flies landing on the horse and circling the zebra without landing.

agreed.text: An adaptation is inherited, and it helps a living thing survive and have young in their own place.
agreed.evidence: Scientists compare the bodies of related plants and animals from different places. The differences match the problems of each place, such as heat, water, cold, hunters and food.

agreed.text: Bright warning colours go with a real defence, and hunters learn to avoid them.
agreed.evidence: In 1869 John Jenner Weir reported that the birds in his aviary ate dull caterpillars and refused bright ones. In the 1960s Lincoln Brower's blue jays vomited after eating monarch butterflies raised on poisonous milkweed, and then refused monarchs.

agreed.text: A harmless mimic is protected only by hunters who have met the model.
agreed.evidence: In 1958 Jane Van Zandt Brower reported tests with Florida scrub jays. Jays who had tasted bitter monarch butterflies refused the look-alike viceroy. Jays who had never met a monarch ate viceroys.

agreed.text: Camouflage lowers the chance of being eaten, and it works only against the right background.
agreed.evidence: Bernard Kettlewell released pale and dark peppered moths in clean and sooty woods in the 1950s. Birds took more of whichever form stood out. From 2001 to 2007 Michael Majerus repeated the work with thousands of moths near Cambridge and found the same.

agreed.text: Predators and prey shape each other over many generations.
agreed.evidence: Collars on wild lions, zebras, cheetahs and impalas showed hunters built for speed and prey built for sharp turns. Moths that live with bats have ears tuned to bat calls.

agreed.text: Living in a group lowers the risk for each animal.
agreed.evidence: In 1971 William Hamilton showed with simple geometry that the edge of a group is more dangerous than the middle. Sheep fitted with trackers move towards the middle of the flock when a dog comes near.

agreed.text: When people change a place quickly, adaptations can fail.
agreed.evidence: Great Indian bustards die on power lines that cross their grassland. Indian vultures died in millions after eating cattle treated with diclofenac.

challenging.claim: A chameleon changes colour to match whatever she sits on.
challenging.for: Chameleons do change colour, and their usual greens and browns match leaves and bark well.
challenging.against: In 2008 Devi Stuart-Fox and Adnan Moussalli studied dwarf chameleons. The biggest and fastest colour changes were signals to other chameleons. Chameleons also change colour as they warm up or cool down.
challenging.context: This card is about a common belief that chameleons change colour mainly to hide.

challenging.claim: A porcupine can shoot her quills at an attacker.
challenging.who: A common belief in many countries.
challenging.for: A dog who attacks a porcupine comes away with quills stuck in the face, as if they had been fired.
challenging.against: The quills are loosely fixed in the skin. The porcupine raises them, rattles them and runs backwards into the attacker. The quills come off when they touch.
challenging.context: This card is about an old belief about how a porcupine uses her quills.

challenging.claim: The viceroy butterfly is a harmless mimic of the bitter monarch.
challenging.who: Textbooks for about a hundred years.
challenging.for: The two butterflies look almost alike, and Jane Brower's jays treated them alike.
challenging.against: In 1991 David Ritland and Lincoln Brower fed both butterflies to red-winged blackbirds. The birds found viceroys as bad-tasting as monarchs. So both are harmful, and each protects the other.
challenging.context: This card is about a famous pair of look-alike butterflies in North America, the monarch and the viceroy.

challenging.claim: An adaptation makes an animal perfect for her place.
challenging.who: A common way of talking about nature.
challenging.for: Many adaptations fit so well that they look designed, such as a camel's nostrils that close.
challenging.against: Every adaptation has a cost, and each one fits the place as it was. A bustard's side-facing eyes suit open grassland and fail her among power lines.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that adapted means perfect.

challenging.claim: Plants are helpless against the animals who eat them.
challenging.for: A plant stays in one spot while a goat or a caterpillar feeds on her.
challenging.against: Plants defend themselves with thorns, tough leaves and bitter chemicals. In 2014 Heidi Appel and Rex Cocroft played the vibrations of a chewing caterpillar to cress plants. When caterpillars later fed on those plants, the plants made more defence chemicals than plants kept in silence.
challenging.context: This card is about whether plants can defend themselves against being eaten.

challenging.claim: A mimic stays safe however many mimics there are.
challenging.for: When the model is very nasty, hunters stay away from the pattern even if mimics are common. Jane Brower found this with starlings and bitter mealworms in 1960.
challenging.against: When the model is only mildly unpleasant, or is missing, hunters soon learn that the pattern is safe. In places with no coral snakes, clay copies of their harmless mimic were attacked more often.
challenging.context: This card is about whether copying a warning works when the copies become common. The Copycat Test in this lesson tests the same question.

big_questions.q: A mimic butterfly is safe because another butterfly is bitter. Whose adaptation is the warning pattern?
big_questions.hint: Think about three animals. The pattern is on the mimic's wings. The poison is in the model's body. And the memory of a bad taste is in the bird.

big_questions.q: A tiger's coat hides her from a deer and stands out to you. Is the tiger camouflaged or not?
big_questions.hint: Ask whether camouflage belongs to the coat, or to the coat and an eye together.

big_questions.q: Deer make tigers stealthy, and tigers make deer watchful. Does either side ever win?
big_questions.hint: Think about what would happen to tigers if they caught every deer.

big_questions.q: People can change a place in ten years. A body changes over thousands of years. What follows from that?
big_questions.hint: Think about the great Indian bustard and the power lines.

big_questions.q: A plant makes her leaves bitter and her ripe fruit sweet. Is she choosing who eats what?
big_questions.hint: In the Bitter Leaf, Sweet Fruit activity in this lesson, you taste a leaf and a ripe fruit and compare them. Also think about a chilli, which burns a rat's mouth but has no effect on a bird's.

big_questions.q: Humans have small teeth, weak claws and slow legs. What are a human's adaptations?
big_questions.hint: Look at your hands and your forward-facing eyes. Think about sweating, talking and making tools.

story.title: The Third Butterfly
story.note: Yazhini, her mother, Vasantha Teacher and the bulbul's visits are made up. These facts are real. The common mormon butterfly lays her eggs on curry leaf and lemon plants all over India. Her young caterpillars look like bird droppings. Older caterpillars are green, with marks like eyes and a forked organ that gives off a sharp smell. The chrysalis is green or brown. The males and some females are black with a row of white spots. Other females copy the common rose, a butterfly who is poisonous because she eats birthwort as a caterpillar. The common rose has a red body, and the copy has a black body. In 2014 Krushnamegh Kunte's team in Bengaluru found that one gene, called doublesex, switches the copied pattern on.
text: Yazhini's mother wanted eight curry leaves for the sambar. Yazhini went to the pot on the balcony and came back with seven leaves and a complaint.
"A bird has dirtied our plant, Amma. In three places."
Her mother came to look. On three leaves sat three small blobs, shiny and brown, each with a smear of white. Then one of the blobs raised a tiny head and began to eat the leaf.
They were caterpillars. Yazhini ran next door to fetch Vasantha Teacher, who taught zoology at the women's college and knew the name of every wing in Madurai.
"Common mormons," said Vasantha Teacher, bending over the pot. "Their mother laid her eggs here last week. Look how well they are dressed. No bulbul wants to eat a bird dropping."
"All three have the same mother?"
"The same mother, on the same morning. I saw her from my window. She was black, with a row of white spots across her wings."
Yazhini's mother agreed to buy her curry leaves from the shop for one month. Yazhini began a diary.

Day 9. They have changed their clothes. They are green now, as green as the leaf, with a brown belt and two painted eyes that are not eyes. I touched one with a twig. A soft red fork shot out of her head, and the whole balcony smelled sharp and sour. I said sorry.

Day 16. They have stopped eating. Each one has spun a belt of silk and is hanging from a twig. Now they are chrysalises. The two on the green stems are green. The one on the dry brown stick is brown. How did she know?
Then nothing happened for eleven days, and Yazhini learned that nothing is the hardest thing to write about.

On the twelfth morning the first chrysalis was empty. A butterfly hung beside the shell, black, with a row of white spots across his wings like a necklace. By evening there was a second butterfly, exactly the same. Yazhini wrote: Day 28. Two brothers. Both like their mother.
The third came out the next morning. Yazhini looked at her for a long time. Then she went next door without her chappals.
"Teacher, the third one is wrong. She has red spots on her wings and a big white patch. She is not a common mormon. Some other butterfly's egg got mixed up in our pot."
Vasantha Teacher did not answer. She took a thick book from her shelf and opened it on the table. On the page was Yazhini's third butterfly: black, with red spots and a white patch.
"There," said Yazhini. "What is she called?"

"That is the common rose. As a caterpillar she eats a poisonous creeper, and she keeps the poison all her life. A bird who eats one is sick. That bird does not touch a second. Now look at the body in the picture."
The body of the common rose was bright red.
"Go and look at yours."
Yazhini went. The third butterfly was still drying her wings on the brown stick. Red spots. White patch. And a body as black as her brothers'.
She walked back slowly, thinking it through.
"She is ours," she said. "She is a mormon. But she is wearing the rose's wings."
"And why would that help her?"
Yazhini thought of the bulbul who sat on the balcony rail every morning, looking into the pot with one eye and then the other.
"Because some day that bulbul will eat a common rose, and be sick. After that she will not stop to check the colour of a body. She will see red spots and remember."
"So what keeps your third butterfly safe?"
"Not her taste. She tastes fine." Yazhini frowned. "The other butterfly keeps her safe. And the bulbul's memory. She is safe because of two animals she has never met."
"Only the daughters dress like this, and not all of them," said Vasantha Teacher. "Nobody is quite sure why. Perhaps you will be the one who finds out."

That evening the two brothers left first, straight up and over the neem tree. Their sister stayed on the rail a little longer. The bulbul landed a metre away. She looked at the red spots with one eye, and then with the other. Then she flew down to the guava tree instead.
Yazhini opened her diary. Day 29, she wrote. Three butterflies, and all of them ours. One is carrying a warning that belongs to somebody else.
story.epiphany: The third butterfly had the wings of the poisonous common rose and the black body of a common mormon. Yazhini saw that the wings were a copied warning. A copy protects only because another animal is truly bitter and a hunter remembers.
ask: Why did the black body show that the third butterfly was a common mormon?
What two things must be true in the garden for the copied wings to protect her?
What might happen to the copycats if common rose butterflies disappeared from Madurai?
