games.title: Catch, Escape or Place? The adaptation cards
games.context: This is a card game about real adaptations. Each card describes one feature of a plant or an animal. You say whether it helps to catch prey, to escape a hunter, or to live in a hard place.

setup.art: Twenty-four cards in a shuffled pile on a table, with three small tokens marked Catch, Escape and Place in front of each player.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile.

setup.art: One child reading a card aloud while another player slides one token forward, face down.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads the front. Everyone else puts down one token, face down.

setup.art: The tokens turned face up and the reader showing the back of the card.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the tokens over. The reader reads the back.

printables.title: 24 adaptation cards: a feature on the front, its job and the reason on the back

items.f: A tiger's two eyes both face forward.
items.b: Catch. Both eyes see the same deer, so the tiger can judge exactly how far to leap.

items.f: A spotted deer's eyes sit on the sides of her head.
items.b: Escape. She sees almost all the way round, so a hunter has few places to hide.

items.f: A barn owl's wing feathers have soft edges like a comb.
items.b: Catch. The soft edges quieten the air, so a mouse does not hear the owl coming.

items.f: A house gecko drops her tail when a cat grabs hold.
items.b: Escape. The tail keeps wriggling and holds the cat's eye while the gecko runs. A new tail grows.

items.f: A camel can close her nostrils to narrow slits.
items.b: Place. Closed nostrils keep blowing sand out in the Thar desert.

items.f: A cactus has spines where other plants have leaves.
items.b: Place and Escape. Spines lose far less water than leaves. They also keep grazing mouths away. Either token scores.

items.f: A deodar's branches slope downwards and bend.
items.b: Place. Snow slides off before its weight can snap the branch.

items.f: A dhole hunts together with her whole pack.
items.b: Catch. Together the pack can tire out a sambar deer who is far bigger than one dhole.

items.f: An Indian pangolin rolls into a ball of hard scales.
items.b: Escape. A leopard's teeth cannot get through the scales.

items.f: A lotus stem is full of air tubes.
items.b: Place. The air keeps the leaf afloat and carries oxygen down to roots in airless mud.

items.f: A Russell's viper has hollow fangs that inject venom.
items.b: Catch. The venom soon stops a rat, so the snake does not have to wrestle her prey.

items.f: A plain tiger butterfly is bright orange and flies slowly in the open.
items.b: Escape. The colour warns birds that she tastes bitter. A bird who has tried one leaves the rest alone.

items.f: A snow leopard has wide, furry paws.
items.b: Place. Wide paws spread her weight on soft snow, and the fur keeps the pads warm.

items.f: A crab spider sitting on a yellow flower is yellow too.
items.b: Catch. A bee does not notice the spider and lands within reach.

items.f: A herd of spotted deer feeds below a troop of langurs.
items.b: Escape. The langurs see far from the treetops and bark when a tiger comes.

items.f: A flamingo has long thin legs and a bent beak that strains water.
items.b: Place. She wades in shallow salty lakes and strains tiny food from the water.

items.f: An Indian crested porcupine rattles her quills and runs backwards at a leopard.
items.b: Escape. The quills come loose and stick in the attacker's face. A porcupine cannot shoot them.

items.f: A mangrove tree stands on arching roots like stilts.
items.b: Place. The stilt roots hold the tree up in soft mud when the tide pulls.

items.f: A cheetah has a bendy spine and a long tail.
items.b: Catch. The spine stretches each stride, and the tail keeps her balanced in a sharp turn.

items.f: A blackbuck leaps and swerves as she runs.
items.b: Escape. A sharp turn at the last moment makes a faster hunter overshoot.

items.f: A female danaid eggfly butterfly looks like the bitter plain tiger.
items.b: Escape. She tastes fine, but birds who have tried a plain tiger leave her alone. This is mimicry.

items.f: A yak has long outer hair over a thick woolly undercoat.
items.b: Place. The double coat traps air and holds her body heat in the cold of Ladakh.

items.f: An archerfish spits a jet of water at an insect on a leaf.
items.b: Catch. The jet knocks the insect into the water. Archerfish live among mangrove roots.

items.f: A touch-me-not plant folds her leaves when something touches them.
items.b: Escape. Scientists think a folded leaf looks small and wilted, so a grazing animal moves on.

printables.title: 3 job tokens: Catch, Escape, Place. Print one set for each player

rules: One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud. The reader keeps the back hidden.
Every other player puts one job token face down. Catch means it helps a hunter. Escape means it helps against being eaten. Place means it helps with heat, cold, water or mud.
Everyone turns the tokens over together. The reader reads the back. Each player whose token matches scores 1 point.
A player who also gives the reason, before the back is read, scores 1 more point. The reader decides, using the back of the card.
With two players, swap the reader's role after every card. The reader does not guess on their own card.
Playing alone? Read a card, say the job and the reason aloud, then turn the card over. Score 1 point for each right job.
After all 24 cards, the player with the most points wins. If you play alone, your score out of 24 is your result.

flow.do: Cut out the 24 cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile. Give each player one set of three tokens.
flow.say: Each card describes one real adaptation. Your three tokens are three jobs: catch prey, escape a hunter, or live in a hard place. We will say which job each adaptation does.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards. Take three tokens.
flow.context: This is the first step of Catch, Escape or Place. You set up the cards and the tokens.

flow.do: Play the first twelve cards. After each card, read the back aloud. Ask the question below after card six.
flow.say: The reader reads the front. Choose a token and put it face down. Say your reason. Now turn the token over, and the reader reads the back. If your token matches the back, you win one point.
flow.kid: Listen to the card. Pick a job token. Say why. Check the back.

ask.q: How did you decide which job the adaptation does?
good: I asked what problem it solves.
I asked whether the animal eats others or is eaten.
I asked whether the problem was a hunter or the weather.

flow.parent: A useful question for a stuck child is: what would go wrong for this animal without this feature? One child can play alone or with you.
flow.context: In this step of Catch, Escape or Place you play the first twelve adaptation cards.

flow.do: Play the last twelve cards the same way. Keep the score on a piece of paper.
flow.say: Twelve more cards. This time, give the reason before the back is read. A good reason earns one more point.
flow.kid: Play twelve more cards. Give your reason before you check.
flow.context: In this step of Catch, Escape or Place you play the last twelve cards and give a reason for each.

flow.do: Count the points. Then lay out the Catch cards in a row. Under each one, try to put an Escape card that answers it.
flow.say: Let us pair the cards. For each Catch card, find an Escape card that works against it. Which Escape card answers the tiger's forward eyes?
flow.kid: Pair each Catch card with an Escape card. Which answers which?

check.q: Which prey adaptation best answers a cheetah's great speed?
options: A sharp swerve at the last moment
check.why: A fast hunter cannot turn tightly, so a swerve makes her overshoot. A call does not move the prey out of reach. A brighter coat helps only an animal who is bitter or can sting.

flow.parent: Good pairs are forward eyes against side eyes, stalking against the langurs' watch, and speed against swerving. Any pair your child can explain is a good pair.
flow.context: This is the last step of Catch, Escape or Place. You pair each hunter's adaptation with a prey adaptation that answers it.

games.title: Bitter or Bluff? A warning game
games.context: This is a bluffing game for two or more players about warning colours. One player is the prey and may put a warning token on any card. The other is the hunter, and decides whether to eat or leave each card.

setup.art: A pile of twenty-four face-down cards on a table with six red and black striped tokens beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the 24 prey cards and the 6 warning tokens. Shuffle the cards.

setup.art: One child holding six cards in her hand and sliding one card face down across the table with a striped token on top of it.
setup.caption: 2. The prey player puts down one card, with or without a warning token.

setup.art: A second child turning over a card that has a striped token on it, while the first child watches.
setup.caption: 3. The hunter says eat or leave. An eaten card is turned over.

printables.title: 24 prey cards: 8 dangerous and 16 harmless
items: DANGEROUS. A plain tiger butterfly. She is bitter from the milkweed she ate as a caterpillar.
DANGEROUS. A common rose butterfly. She is poisonous from the birthwort she ate as a caterpillar.
DANGEROUS. A crimson rose butterfly. She is poisonous, like her cousin the common rose.
DANGEROUS. A yellow paper wasp. She stings.
DANGEROUS. A rock bee. She stings, and her sisters come to help.
DANGEROUS. An orange and black blister beetle. Her body fluid burns the mouth.
DANGEROUS. A painted grasshopper. She is poisonous from the milkweed she eats.
DANGEROUS. A banded krait. Her bite is venomous.
HARMLESS. A female danaid eggfly butterfly. In real life she copies the plain tiger.
HARMLESS. A female common mormon butterfly. In real life some copy the common rose.
HARMLESS. A hoverfly. In real life she is striped like a wasp, but she has no sting.
HARMLESS. A common wolf snake. She has pale bands like a krait, but no venom.
HARMLESS. A rat snake. She has no venom.

printables.title: 6 warning tokens. Colour them with red and black stripes

rules: Shuffle the 24 cards. One player is the prey and takes 6 cards. The prey looks at them. The other player is the hunter and does not see them.
The prey puts one card face down in front of the hunter. The prey may put a warning token on it.
The truth rule: a DANGEROUS card must always carry a warning token. A HARMLESS card may carry one too. That is a bluff.
The hunter says 'eat' or 'leave'. If the hunter eats, turn the card over. A harmless card gives the hunter 1 point. A dangerous card takes 2 points from the hunter.
If the hunter leaves the card, it stays face down, and the prey scores 1 point.
After 6 cards, turn over the cards that were left, to see which were bluffs. Then swap roles and deal 6 new cards.
Play until all 24 cards are used, so each player is the prey twice. The player with the most points wins.
With three or four players, take turns as the prey. The player on the prey's left is the hunter.

flow.do: Cut out the 24 cards and the 6 tokens. Colour the tokens with red and black stripes, or use six red buttons instead. Read the rules together and shuffle the cards.
flow.say: In this game a warning token says 'I am dangerous'. A dangerous card must always carry one. A harmless card may carry one too, as a bluff. The hunter must decide whether to believe it.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Make the tokens red, as a warning. Shuffle the cards.
flow.context: This is the first step of Bitter or Bluff. You make the cards and the warning tokens and learn the rules.

flow.do: Play the first two deals. Your child is the prey first, and then the hunter. Write down each player's points after each deal.
flow.say: You are the prey first. Put down one card at a time, with a token or without. I am the hunter, and I will say eat or leave.
flow.kid: Play two deals. Be the prey first. Then be the hunter.
flow.parent: Do not explain any tactics yet. Let your child find out what happens when they bluff a lot or a little.
flow.context: In this step of Bitter or Bluff you play the first two deals. You are the prey once and the hunter once.

flow.do: Play the last two deals. Before you start, ask the question below. After each deal, turn over the cards that were left and count the bluffs.
flow.say: Before we go on, think about the first two deals. How often did the prey bluff? Did the hunter start eating cards with tokens? Now play two more deals and watch for that.
flow.kid: Play two more deals. Count the bluffs after each deal.

ask.q: What happened when the prey put a token on almost every card?
good: The hunter stopped believing the tokens.
The hunter ate some and found they were harmless.
The tokens stopped working.

flow.context: In this step of Bitter or Bluff you play the last two deals and count how many warnings were bluffs.

flow.do: Add up the points and name the winner. Then talk about the questions below.
flow.say: Who won? When did a bluff work best for the prey? In nature, a harmless fly called a hoverfly bluffs with a wasp's stripes. What would happen if hoverflies became far more common than wasps?
flow.kid: Add up the points. When did a bluff work best?

check.q: When does a false warning protect a harmless animal best?
options: When most warnings around are true
When every animal gives the warning
check.why: A hunter believes a warning only if it is usually true. If every animal bluffs, or none is dangerous, the hunter learns that the warning means nothing and eats.

flow.parent: In the game, a third of the cards are dangerous. A prey player who bluffs on a few cards is usually believed. One who bluffs on every card is soon tested.
flow.context: This is the last step of Bitter or Bluff. You add up the points and work out when a bluff is believed.

experiments.title: The Snow Load Test: which tree shape carries the least snow?
experiments.context: In this experiment you make three paper trees: one flat, one a low cone and one a steep cone. You pour rava on each as snow, and measure how much stays on.
experiments.question: Ten level teaspoons of rava are poured on the top of a paper tree. How much stays on a flat tree, on a low cone and on a steep cone?
experiments.predict: Before you pour, guess. Which paper tree will keep the most rava snow, and which will keep the least? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Cut all three trees from circles of the same size and the same paper. Pour the same 10 level teaspoons on each tree. Pour from the same height, about 10 centimetres, onto the very top. Stand every tree on the same upturned tumbler. Test each tree twice, because one pour can be a fluke. Only the slope of the tree changes.
results_table: Teaspoons of snow that stayed on, try 1
Teaspoons of snow that stayed on, try 2

materials.item: sheets of stiff paper, such as old calendar pages, chart paper or magazine covers
a small plate or a vessel lid about 18 centimetres across, to draw round
a pencil, scissors and sticky tape
dry rava (sooji), about half a cup. Fine salt or sugar also works
a teaspoon
a steel tumbler, to stand upside down as the trunk
a large plate or tray, to catch the rava that slides off
a small bowl, and a notebook page for the results

experiments.record: Draw a table with three rows, for the flat tree, the low cone and the steep cone. For each tree, write how many teaspoons stayed on in try 1 and in try 2. Measure to the nearest half teaspoon.

example_chart.title: Made-up example: teaspoons of rava that stayed on, out of 10

setup.art: Three paper circles on a table, each folded and opened so that eight slice lines show, with a small plate, a pencil and scissors beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Cut three paper circles. Fold each one to mark eight equal slices.

setup.art: Three paper trees in a row: a flat circle, a low wide cone and a tall steep cone, each taped along one edge.
setup.caption: 2. Leave one flat. Overlap one slice for the low cone. Overlap four slices for the steep cone.

setup.art: A flat paper circle resting on an upturned steel tumbler in the middle of a large plate, with a hand pouring rava from a teaspoon onto the middle.
setup.caption: 3. Stand a tree on the upturned tumbler. Pour 10 level teaspoons of rava on the top.

setup.art: A child tipping the rava left on a paper cone into a small bowl, with a teaspoon ready to measure it.
setup.caption: 4. Tip what stayed on into a bowl. Count it back in level teaspoons.

setup.art: A notebook table with three rows named Flat tree, Low cone and Steep cone, and numbers in two columns.
setup.caption: 5. Write the result. Test each tree twice.

flow.do: Show your child the paper, the tumbler and the rava. Describe the three trees you will make. Ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: We will make three paper trees: a flat one, a low cone and a steep cone. Rava will be our snow. Which tree will keep the most snow on top, and which the least?
flow.kid: Guess which paper tree keeps the most rava snow, and which keeps the least.

ask.q: Why do you think that tree will keep the least snow?
good: The snow will slide down the steep sides.
There is no flat place for it to sit.
It is like a slide in the park.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Snow Load Test. You guess which paper tree will keep the most rava snow, before you test.

flow.do: Draw round the plate three times and cut out the circles. Fold each circle in half three times, then open it. The folds mark eight slices. Leave the first circle flat. On the other two, cut along one fold from the edge to the centre. Slide one cut edge over the next slice on the second circle, and tape it. On the third, slide it over four slices, and tape it.
flow.say: All three trees start as the same circle. The flat tree stays a flat circle. The low cone has one slice tucked under. The steep cone has four slices tucked under, which is half the circle.
flow.kid: Cut three circles. Fold each into eight slices. Make one flat tree. Make a low cone. Make a steep cone.

check.q: Why are all three paper trees cut from circles of the same size?
options: So that only the slope differs
So that the rava weighs less
check.why: A fair test changes one thing only. With the same paper and the same circle, the only difference between the trees is how steep they are. If you chose 'so that they look neat', remember that neatness does not change the result.

flow.parent: Stiff paper keeps its shape best. If you have only thin paper, tape two sheets together before you cut.
flow.context: In this step of the Snow Load Test you cut three equal paper circles. You turn them into a flat tree, a low cone and a steep cone.

flow.do: Stand the tumbler upside down in the middle of the tray. Rest the flat tree on the tumbler. Pour 10 level teaspoons of rava onto the middle, one at a time, from about 10 centimetres above. Lift the tree and tip the rava that stayed on into the bowl. Count it back in level teaspoons and record it. Do this twice.
flow.say: This is the flat tree. Pour ten level teaspoons on the middle, slowly. Now lift the paper carefully and tip the snow into the bowl. How many teaspoons stayed on?
flow.kid: Pour ten teaspoons on the flat tree. Tip what stayed into the bowl. Count it.
flow.parent: Pour the rava from the tray back into the cup after each try, so that none is wasted.
flow.context: In this step of the Snow Load Test you pour 10 teaspoons of rava on the flat paper tree. Then you measure how much stays on.

flow.do: Put the low cone on the tumbler like a hat. Pour 10 level teaspoons of rava onto the tip, from the same height. Measure what stayed on, and record it. Do this twice.
flow.say: Now the low cone. Pour onto the very tip, from the same height as before. Watch what the rava does when it lands. How many teaspoons stayed on this time?
flow.kid: Pour ten teaspoons on the low cone. Watch the rava. Count what stayed.

ask.q: What did you see the rava do on the low cone?
good: Some stayed in a heap at the top.
It piled up and then slid down in a rush.
Some rolled off the edge.

flow.parent: The low cone gives the most varied results. On shiny paper most of the rava slides off. On rough paper a heap stays near the tip.
flow.context: In this step of the Snow Load Test you pour 10 teaspoons of rava on the low paper cone. Then you measure how much stays on.

flow.do: Put the steep cone on the tumbler. Pour 10 level teaspoons of rava onto the tip, from the same height. Measure what stayed on, and record it. Do this twice.
flow.say: Last, the steep cone. Pour onto the tip again. How many teaspoons stayed on?
flow.kid: Pour ten teaspoons on the steep cone. Count what stayed.
flow.context: In this step of the Snow Load Test you pour 10 teaspoons of rava on the steep paper cone. Then you measure how much stays on.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Look at your table. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Now think of a real tree. What would a heavy load of snow do to a wide, flat branch?
flow.kid: Look at your table. Which tree kept the most rava? Which kept the least?

ask.q: Why did the steep cone keep so little rava?
good: The slope was too steep for the grains to stay.
Each grain slid or rolled down.
There was nothing flat to hold a heap.

ask.q: A banyan grows wide and flat-topped. Why is that shape a good one in Chennai?
good: There is no snow there.
A wide tree catches more sunlight.
Her leaves spread out to the light.

flow.parent: In most homes the flat tree keeps nearly all 10 teaspoons and the steep cone keeps less than 1. The low cone is in between. Write down what you really found. The reason: the paper grips each grain, and the grain's weight drags it down the slope. On a steep slope the weight wins, and the grain slides. Firs, spruces and young deodars on Himalayan slopes are narrow cones, and their branches slope down and bend. Snow slides off before its weight can break them. A wide crown catches more light, so trees in warm places can spread out. Wet snow is stickier than rava, so real trees need bendy branches as well as steep ones.
flow.think: A steep cone sheds snow, but it is narrow and catches less light from above. How could a tree do both?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Snow Load Test. You compare how much rava stayed on the flat tree, the low cone and the steep cone, and say why.

experiments.title: The Copycat Test: is a copied warning still safe when copycats are common?
experiments.context: In this experiment a hunter turns over paper squares to score points. Some patterned squares are bitter and some are harmless copycats. You find out whether copycats are safer when they are few or when they are many.
experiments.question: A hunter learns that a pattern means a bitter taste. Does the hunter leave harmless copycats alone when 2 patterned squares in 12 are copycats? What about when 10 in 12 are copycats?
experiments.predict: Before the hunts, guess. One hunt has few copycats among the patterned squares, and the other has many. In which hunt will more copycats be left alive? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use 16 squares of the same paper in each hunt: 4 plain and 12 with a pattern. Keep the scores the same in both hunts: plus 1 for a tasty square and minus 2 for a bitter one. The same person is the hunter both times, with the same rule. Only the share of copycats changes, from 2 in 12 to 10 in 12. The pattern also changes from stripes to dots, so that the hunter starts each hunt without a habit. Say so when you report your result.

materials.item: sheets of plain notebook paper, each cut into 16 pieces
a red or orange crayon or sketch pen, to draw the stripes and the dots
a pencil, to write a small T or B under each square
a sheet of newspaper to lay the squares on, so that the letters do not show through
scissors, and a notebook page for the results

experiments.record: Draw a table with two rows, one for each hunt. Write how many patterned squares the hunter ate out of 12. Write how many copycats were eaten and how many were left alive. Write the hunter's score.

setup.art: Thirty-two small paper pieces on a table in two groups of sixteen, one group with twelve pieces marked with red stripes and the other with twelve pieces marked with red dots.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up makes two sets of 16 squares: 4 plain and 12 patterned in each.

setup.art: The underside of several paper squares, each with a small pencil letter T or B.
setup.caption: 2. Under each square is a T for tasty or a B for bitter. The hunter must not see.

setup.art: A child turning over one striped paper square from sixteen squares spread on a newspaper.
setup.caption: 3. The hunter turns over one square at a time, and may stop at any time.

setup.art: All the squares turned over after the hunt, and a notebook table with two rows of numbers.
setup.caption: 4. After each hunt, turn over the rest. Count the copycats left alive.

flow.do: Explain the hunt. Your child will be the hunter. Tell them the scores, and that one hunt has few copycats and the other has many. Do not say which. Ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: You will be a hungry bird. A tasty square scores plus 1 and a bitter square scores minus 2. Some bitter squares carry a pattern. Tasty squares that copy the pattern are copycats. One hunt has few copycats and one has many. In which hunt will more copycats be left alive? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: You are the hunter. One hunt has few copycats and one has many. Guess where copycats are safer.

ask.q: Why do you think copycats will be safer in that hunt?
good: If most patterned ones are bitter, I will stop eating them.
If most are tasty, I will keep eating them.
The copycats hide among the bitter ones.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Copycat Test. You guess whether harmless copycats are safer when they are few or when they are many.

flow.do: Send your child to draw the results table in another room. Cut each sheet into 16 pieces. For hunt 1, draw three thick stripes on 12 pieces and leave 4 plain. Underneath, write B on 10 striped pieces, and T on 2 striped pieces and on the 4 plain ones. For hunt 2, draw three big dots on 12 pieces and leave 4 plain. Underneath, write B on 2 dotted pieces, and T on 10 dotted pieces and on the 4 plain ones.
flow.say: Please draw the results table while I make the prey. It needs two rows and five columns. I will call you when both sets are ready.
flow.kid: Draw the results table in another room. A grown-up makes the paper prey.
flow.parent: Draw all the patterns first and write the letters afterwards, so that copycats and bitter squares look exactly alike. Write the letters small and in pencil. Lay the hunt 1 squares on the newspaper, pattern side up and well mixed. Keep hunt 2 out of sight.
flow.context: In this step of the Copycat Test a grown-up secretly makes two sets of paper prey. The first set has 2 copycats and the second has 10.

flow.do: Lay the hunt 1 squares pattern side up on the newspaper, well mixed. Call your child. Read out the rules. They turn over one square at a time and keep a running score. They may stop whenever they like. Put the eaten squares in a pile.
flow.say: Here is the first forest. Turn over one square at a time. T is tasty and scores plus 1. B is bitter and scores minus 2. Stop whenever you like. Try to finish with the highest score you can.
flow.kid: Turn over one square at a time. T scores 1. B loses 2. Stop when you like.

check.q: In the Copycat Test, why does a bitter square take away 2 points?
options: A bad meal costs a real bird something
check.why: A bird who eats bitter prey may be sick and loses time for feeding. The minus 2 stands for that cost. Without a cost, the hunter would have no reason to avoid any square.

flow.parent: A curious child may want to turn over every square. Remind them that the aim is the highest score.
flow.context: In this step of the Copycat Test you hunt the first set of paper prey, where 12 squares have stripes.

flow.do: Count the striped squares in the eaten pile, and how many of them were copycats marked T. Then turn over all the squares left on the newspaper. Count the striped copycats left alive. Record the numbers and the score.
flow.say: Let us count. How many striped squares did you eat out of 12? How many of them were copycats? Now turn over the rest. How many copycats are still alive?
flow.kid: Count the striped squares you ate. Turn over the rest. Count the copycats alive.
flow.context: In this step of the Copycat Test you count the striped copycats eaten and left alive in the first hunt.

flow.do: Clear the newspaper. Lay out the hunt 2 squares, pattern side up and well mixed. Your child hunts again with the same rules.
flow.say: This is a different forest. The dotted prey here are a different kind of animal, so you know nothing about them yet. The scores are the same. Find out what you can, and get the highest score.
flow.kid: This is a new forest with dotted prey. Hunt again. Get your best score.
flow.context: In this step of the Copycat Test you hunt the second set of paper prey, where 12 squares have dots.

flow.do: Count the dotted squares in the eaten pile, and how many of them were copycats. Turn over the squares that are left. Count the dotted copycats left alive. Record the numbers and the score.
flow.say: Count again. How many dotted squares did you eat out of 12? How many copycats were eaten, and how many are still alive?
flow.kid: Count the dotted squares you ate. Count the copycats left alive.
flow.context: In this step of the Copycat Test you count the dotted copycats eaten and left alive in the second hunt.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Look at your two rows. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. The copycats looked the same as the bitter squares in both hunts. So what made them safe in one hunt and not in the other?
flow.kid: Compare your two rows. In which hunt were more copycats left alive?

ask.q: Why did you stop eating striped squares in the first hunt?
good: The first ones I tried were bitter.
I lost points, so I learned to avoid stripes.
It was not worth the risk.

ask.q: What does a copycat need, in order to be left alone?
good: Plenty of really bitter animals with the same pattern.
A hunter who has tasted the bitter kind.
Not too many other copycats.

flow.parent: Most hunters eat only 1 to 3 striped squares in the first hunt, so both striped copycats usually live. In the second hunt most hunters find that dotted squares are nearly all tasty, and eat most of them. Write down what you really found. A careful hunter may stop early in both hunts, and real birds differ in the same way. The reason: a hunter judges a pattern by the meals it has given so far. When most patterned prey are bitter, the hunter avoids the pattern, and the few copycats are protected. When most are harmless, the hunter learns that the pattern is safe. So a copycat depends on the bitter animals whose pattern she copies. Scientists call the copycat a mimic and the bitter animal a model. Jane Brower tested this in 1960 with starlings and bitter mealworms.
flow.think: Make 12 new squares with a third pattern. How many of them must be bitter before a hunter gives up on that pattern?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Copycat Test. You compare the copycats left alive in the two hunts, and say why.

activities.title: Front Eyes or Side Eyes: sort twelve animals
activities.context: In this activity you look at where your own eyes point. Then you sort twelve animals by where their eyes are, and look for a pattern in what they eat.

materials.item: a mirror
a notebook page and a pencil
any pictures of animals you have, such as a book, a calendar or the adaptation cards (you can also work from memory)

activities.record: A table with two columns, 'Eyes at the front' and 'Eyes at the sides'. Write each of the twelve animals in one column, and beside each animal write what they mostly eat.

setup.art: A child looking into a mirror and pointing with both forefingers in the direction her two eyes are looking.
setup.caption: 1. Look in a mirror. Both your eyes point forward.

setup.art: A notebook page with two columns headed Eyes at the front and Eyes at the sides, with animal names in each.
setup.caption: 2. Sort twelve animals into two columns. Write what each one eats.

setup.art: The face of a cat seen from the front beside the head of a goat seen from the front, showing the cat's eyes facing forward and the goat's eyes on the sides.
setup.caption: 3. Look for the pattern. Then look for the animals who do not fit.

flow.do: Your child looks in the mirror and notes where both eyes point. Then they look straight ahead and cover one eye with a hand. Ask what changed.
flow.say: Look at your face in the mirror. Where do your two eyes point? Now look straight ahead and cover one eye. How much of the room did you lose? Which animals do you think have eyes placed like yours?
flow.kid: Look in the mirror. Where do your eyes point? Cover one eye. What changed?
flow.parent: With one eye covered, only a strip at the far side disappears. Most of what one eye sees, the other eye sees too.
flow.context: This is the first step of Front Eyes or Side Eyes. You find out where your own two eyes point and how much both of them see.

flow.do: Write these twelve animals on slips of paper, or use pictures: tiger, house cat, owl, bonnet macaque, human, cow, goat, spotted deer, rabbit, pigeon, hen and fish. Lay two columns on the table, 'Eyes at the front' and 'Eyes at the sides', and sort the slips. Then ask what each animal mostly eats, and write the answer on that animal's slip.
flow.say: Put each animal in a column: eyes at the front, or eyes at the sides. Use pictures or your memory. Then say what each one mostly eats.
flow.kid: Sort twelve animals by where their eyes are. Say what each one eats.
flow.parent: Front: tiger, house cat, owl, bonnet macaque and human. Sides: cow, goat, spotted deer, rabbit, pigeon, hen and most fish. If your child is unsure about one, look for a picture together.
flow.context: In this step of Front Eyes or Side Eyes you sort twelve animals by where their eyes are. You also write what each one eats.

flow.do: Look at the two columns together. Ask the questions below. Then do the check.
flow.say: Look down the front column. What do most of those animals eat? Look down the side column. Who hunts those animals? Two animals in the front column are not hunters. Which are they, and why might their eyes face forward?
flow.kid: What do the front-eyed animals eat? Which two do not fit?

ask.q: Why might a monkey need eyes that face forward?
good: She jumps between branches and must judge the distance.
She picks fruit with her fingers.
Two eyes on one thing tell her how far it is.

check.q: What do eyes at the front of the face do best?
options: Judge how far away one thing is
See what is behind the head
check.why: Two eyes that look at the same thing give the brain two views, and the brain works out the distance. A hunter must judge distance to pounce, and so must a monkey to jump. Eyes at the sides see more of the surroundings, and judge distance less well.

flow.parent: The pattern is strong but not perfect, and the exceptions show what forward eyes are really for: judging distance. Monkeys and humans come from ancestors who leapt between branches.
flow.context: This is the last step of Front Eyes or Side Eyes. You look for the pattern linking the place of the eyes to what an animal eats.

activities.title: Edge or Middle: where in a herd is the safest place?
activities.context: In this activity 19 chickpeas, called chana, are a herd of deer and a rolling marble is a tiger. You count which deer the tiger reaches first, and compare a deer in a herd with a deer alone.

materials.item: dry chana, or peanuts or rajma
a marble, or a small ball of dough about as wide as your thumb
a large sheet of paper or newspaper on a smooth floor or table
a dice, or six folded slips of paper numbered 1 to 6
a pencil and a notebook page

activities.record: A tally with three rows: edge, inner ring and centre. Put one stroke each time a chana in that place is caught. Then a second tally for the chana who stands alone.

setup.art: Nineteen chana on a sheet of paper arranged as one in the middle, a ring of six around it and a ring of twelve outside, with six numbered pencil marks around the whole herd.
setup.caption: 1. Arrange 19 chana in three rings. Mark six start points around them.

setup.art: A child rolling a marble from a numbered mark towards the herd of chana, with a dice beside her.
setup.caption: 2. Roll the dice for a start point. Roll the marble at the middle of the herd.

setup.art: A notebook tally with many strokes in the row named Edge and none in the rows named Inner ring and Centre.
setup.caption: 3. The first chana touched is caught. Put a stroke in the tally and put her back.

flow.do: Put 1 chana in the middle of the paper. Put 6 around it, each a finger-width away. Put 12 around those, a finger-width further out. Mark six start points around the herd, each a hand-span from the outer ring. Number them 1 to 6. Ask for a guess.
flow.say: These 19 chana are a herd of deer. The marble is a tiger, who rushes in from any side. Which deer do you think the tiger will catch most often: one at the edge, one in the inner ring, or the one in the centre? Why?
flow.kid: Arrange the herd in three rings. Guess where the tiger will catch most.
flow.context: This is the first step of Edge or Middle. You arrange 19 chana as a herd and guess which place is most dangerous.

flow.do: Roll the dice to choose a start point. Roll the marble from there at the middle of the herd. The first chana the marble touches is caught. Put a stroke in the tally and put the chana back. Do this 12 times.
flow.say: Roll the dice for the tiger's side. Now roll the marble at the middle of the herd. Which deer did the tiger touch first? Mark it in the tally and put her back in place.
flow.kid: Roll the dice. Roll the marble at the herd. Tally who was caught. Do twelve attacks.
flow.parent: The gaps between the chana are narrower than the marble, so the marble nearly always touches an edge chana first.
flow.context: In this step of Edge or Middle you roll a marble tiger at the chana herd 12 times. You tally which chana is touched first.

flow.do: Count the tally. Then take the herd away and leave 1 chana alone on the paper. Ask how many of 12 attacks would catch her. Talk about the questions below.
flow.say: How many attacks caught an edge deer? How many caught the centre deer? Now one deer stands alone. If the tiger attacks 12 times, how often is she the one who is caught? So which is safer: alone, at the edge, or in the middle?
flow.kid: Count the tally. Now one chana stands alone. How often is she caught?

ask.q: There were 12 attacks and 12 edge deer. About how many times was each edge deer caught?
good: About once each.
12 attacks shared among 12 deer is 1 each.

ask.q: If every deer tries to get to the middle, what happens to the herd?
good: The herd packs tightly together.
Somebody is always left on the edge.
The slow or weak ones end up outside.

check.q: Twelve attacks come. Who is caught more often: a deer alone, or one deer in a herd?
check.why: A deer alone is the only target, so every successful attack takes her. In the herd, the attacks are shared among many, so each deer's share is small. This is one reason why prey animals live in groups.

flow.parent: Two ideas come out of the tally. In a group each animal's risk is shared, and the middle is safer than the edge. Fish in a shoal and sheep near a dog both crowd towards the middle.
flow.context: This is the last step of Edge or Middle. You compare the risk at the edge, in the middle and alone.

activities.title: Bitter Leaf, Sweet Fruit: what a plant lets you eat
activities.context: In this activity you taste a ripe fruit, a leaf and an unripe fruit from the kitchen. You work out which parts a plant defends and which part she offers to animals.

materials.item: a ripe banana, or another ripe fruit
a bitter or strong-tasting kitchen leaf or vegetable: a methi leaf, a thin slice of karela or a curry leaf
an unripe fruit if you have one: a slice of raw mango, green guava or raw banana
a plant part with thorns, hairs or a tough skin to look at: a lemon twig, a brinjal stalk or a lady's finger
a knife for the grown-up, a plate, drinking water and a notebook page

activities.safety: Taste only the kitchen foods named here. Never taste a wild plant, an unknown berry or milky sap. A grown-up does the cutting.
activities.record: A table with one row for each thing you taste. Write the part of the plant and the taste. Then give a score from 1 to 5 for how much an animal would want more.

setup.art: A plate with a slice of ripe banana, a methi leaf, a thin slice of karela and a slice of raw green mango, each with a small label.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up cuts small pieces: a ripe fruit, a leaf and an unripe fruit.

setup.art: A child tasting a tiny piece of a green leaf and making a face, with a tumbler of water beside her.
setup.caption: 2. Taste a tiny piece of each. Sip water in between.

setup.art: A notebook table with rows for ripe fruit, leaf and unripe fruit, and a score from 1 to 5 beside each.
setup.caption: 3. Score each one. Would an animal come back for more?

flow.do: Cut a small piece of each food and put the pieces on a plate. Ask your child which part of the plant each piece is. Ask for a guess before any tasting.
flow.say: Each of these is a part of a plant. Which is a leaf, and which is a fruit? A plant stays in one spot while animals feed on her. Which of these parts do you think the plant most needs to protect? Why?
flow.kid: Name each plant part. Which part does a plant most need to protect? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of Bitter Leaf, Sweet Fruit. You name the plant parts on the plate and guess which ones a plant protects.

flow.do: Your child tastes a tiny piece of the ripe fruit, then the leaf, then the unripe fruit. They sip water in between. For each one they write the taste and a score from 1 to 5.
flow.say: Taste a tiny piece of the ripe fruit first. Then the leaf. Then the unripe fruit. After each one, say the taste. Then give a score from 1 to 5 for how much an animal would want to eat more.
flow.kid: Taste a tiny piece of each. Sip water in between. Score each from 1 to 5.
flow.parent: Your child may spit out the bitter piece. The ripe fruit usually scores 4 or 5. The leaf and the unripe fruit usually score 1 or 2.
flow.context: In this step of Bitter Leaf, Sweet Fruit you taste a ripe fruit, a leaf and an unripe fruit. You score each one.

flow.do: Look at the lemon twig, the brinjal stalk or the lady's finger. Find thorns, hairs or a tough skin. Do not taste these.
flow.say: Taste is one defence. Look for others. Can you find thorns, tiny hairs or a tough skin? Which animals would each one keep away?
flow.kid: Look for thorns, hairs and tough skin. Who would they keep away?
flow.context: In this step of Bitter Leaf, Sweet Fruit you look for a plant's other defences, such as thorns and hairs.

flow.do: Talk about the questions below. Read your child the explanation in the note after they have answered.
flow.say: Look at your scores. Which part did the plant make pleasant to eat? Which parts did she make unpleasant?
flow.kid: Look at your scores. Which part would an animal come back to?

ask.q: What does a plant gain when an animal eats her ripe fruit?
good: The animal carries the seeds away.
The seeds come out in droppings somewhere new.

ask.q: Why is an unripe fruit sour or bitter, and green?
good: The seeds are not ready yet.
Green hides the fruit among the leaves.
The plant keeps eaters away until the seeds can grow.

check.q: Which part of a plant is most often made sweet for animals to eat?
check.why: A ripe fruit is the plant's payment to animals who carry her seeds away. Leaves make the plant's food, so many plants make them bitter or tough. An unripe fruit is defended until the seeds are ready.

flow.parent: Leaves make the plant's food, so many plants defend them with bitter chemicals, hairs or thorns. A ripe fruit is different. It is sweet and brightly coloured, and it invites animals who will carry the seeds away. An unripe fruit is sour and green until the seeds are ready. The chilli is a special case. The burning chemical in a chilli hurts the mouths of rats and other mammals, who would crush the seeds. The sensors in a bird's mouth do not respond to that chemical. Birds swallow the seeds whole and spread them.
flow.context: This is the last step of Bitter Leaf, Sweet Fruit. You work out why a plant makes her leaves unpleasant and her ripe fruit sweet.

activities.title: Warning Colours at Home: who uses red, yellow and black?
activities.context: In this activity you hunt around your home and street for the colours people use to mean danger. You compare them with the warning colours of wasps and butterflies.

materials.item: a notebook page and a pencil
your home, and a window or balcony that looks on to a street

activities.record: A list of every danger sign or warning mark you find. Beside each one, write its colours and what it warns about.

setup.art: A child looking at the red warning mark on a bottle of floor cleaner on a high shelf, without touching it.
setup.caption: 1. Hunt for warning marks at home. Look, and do not touch.

setup.art: A view from a window of a street with a yellow and black road barrier, a yellow school bus and a red danger sign on an electricity box.
setup.caption: 2. Look at the street from a window. Add what you see.

setup.art: A notebook list of warning marks with a tally of colours beside it: red, yellow, black and others.
setup.caption: 3. Tally the colours. Which ones come up most?

flow.do: Ask your child which colours they expect to find on danger signs, and why. Write the guess down.
flow.say: People put warning marks on things that can hurt us. Which colours do you think we will find most often on them? Why those colours?
flow.kid: Which colours mean danger on signs? Guess, and say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of Warning Colours at Home. You guess which colours people use on danger signs.

flow.do: Walk round the home together for five minutes, and look out of a window. List every warning mark: on cleaners, medicines, the gas cylinder, the electricity meter, road barriers, buses and autos. Look and do not touch.
flow.say: Find every mark that warns of danger. Look at the cleaning bottles, the medicine strips, the gas cylinder and the meter box. Then look at the street. Write each one with its colours.
flow.kid: Hunt for warning marks for five minutes. Write each one with its colours.
flow.parent: Good finds: the red gas cylinder, the red line on some medicine strips and the danger sign on a meter box. On the street, look for yellow and black road barriers and yellow school buses.
flow.context: In this step of Warning Colours at Home you list the warning marks in your home and on your street. You note their colours.

flow.do: Tally the colours. Talk about the questions below.
flow.say: Which colours came up most? A wasp is yellow and black, and a plain tiger butterfly is orange and black. Do those match our danger marks?
flow.kid: Count how many times each colour came up. Which colour won?

ask.q: Why are red, yellow and black good for a warning?
good: They stand out against green and brown.
You can see them from far away.
A bold pattern is easy to remember.

ask.q: What would happen if every bottle had a red danger mark?
good: Nobody would take the mark seriously.
The mark would stop meaning danger.
It is like too many copycats.

flow.parent: People and insects face the same problem: a warning must be seen from far off and remembered. A warning mark also stops working if it is put on harmless things. In the Copycat Test experiment, the hunter ate the dotted squares once most of them proved harmless.
flow.context: This is the last step of Warning Colours at Home. You tally the colours and compare people's warnings with the warning colours of insects.

activities.title: Turn or Sprint: can a slower runner escape? (if you have a terrace, a corridor or a park)
activities.context: In this activity a faster chaser tries to tag a slower runner before a finish line. You compare running straight with turning sharply, as a blackbuck does when a cheetah is close.

materials.item: a clear space about 15 big steps long, such as a terrace, a long corridor or a park
two chappals or bottles to mark the start and the finish
a faster chaser (a grown-up or an older child) and a slower runner
a notebook page and a pencil

activities.safety: Use a dry floor with nothing to trip over. Keep well away from stairs and from the edge of a terrace. Tag gently on the shoulder.
activities.record: A table with two rows, 'Straight run' and 'Run with turns'. For each of 3 tries, write 'tagged' or 'escaped'.

setup.art: A terrace with two chappals marking a start line and a finish line about fifteen steps apart.
setup.caption: 1. Mark a start and a finish, 15 big steps apart.

setup.art: A child standing three steps ahead of a grown-up, both ready to run in the same direction.
setup.caption: 2. The runner starts 3 steps ahead of the faster chaser.

setup.art: A child swerving sharply to one side while a grown-up running behind overshoots in a straight line.
setup.caption: 3. Try three straight runs. Then try three runs with sharp turns.

flow.do: Mark the start and the finish. The runner stands 3 big steps ahead of the chaser. Ask for a guess.
flow.say: I am the cheetah and I am faster than you. You are the blackbuck, with a start of three steps. Can you reach the finish before I tag you, if you run straight? What if you are allowed to turn? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: The chaser is faster. Can you escape by running straight? By turning? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of Turn or Sprint. You set up a chase between a faster chaser and a slower runner, and guess who wins.

flow.do: Do 3 straight runs. The runner must run in a straight line to the finish. Record 'tagged' or 'escaped' each time. Rest between runs.
flow.say: First, three straight runs. You must not turn. Ready, go.
flow.kid: Run straight to the finish three times. Write tagged or escaped.
flow.context: In this step of Turn or Sprint the slower runner runs straight three times. You record whether the chaser tags them.

flow.do: Do 3 runs with turns. The runner may swerve sharply whenever the chaser is close, but must still reach the finish. Record each run. Then talk about the questions below.
flow.say: Now you may swerve when I get close. Wait until the last moment, and then turn sharply. Ready, go.
flow.kid: Now swerve when the chaser is close. Did you escape more often?

ask.q: What happened to the chaser when you turned sharply?
good: They ran past me.
They could not turn as fast.
They had to slow down first.

flow.parent: A faster and heavier body needs more room to turn, so the chaser overshoots. Most families find more escapes with turns than without. Scientists who put collars on cheetahs and impalas found the same. The prey escaped by slowing a little and turning sharply.
flow.context: This is the last step of Turn or Sprint. The slower runner is allowed to swerve, and you compare the result with the straight runs.

projects.title: An Animal at Risk: when the place changes faster than the body
projects.context: In this three-day project you choose one Indian animal who is at risk. You find out what place her body is fitted to, what people changed there, and what could be done.

materials.item: sheets of plain paper, or one sheet of chart paper
pencils and colour pens
a library book, a children's encyclopaedia or trusted websites, used with a grown-up

schedule.what: Choose the animal. Find out where she lives and three of her adaptations.
Find out what people changed in her place, with one number as evidence.
Make a one-page poster with four boxes, and give a three-minute talk.

projects.record: A one-page poster with four boxes: her place, her adaptations, what changed, and what people can do. One number as evidence in the third box.

setup.art: A child and a parent looking at a book open at a picture of a great Indian bustard, with a notebook beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Choose one Indian animal at risk. Find her place and three adaptations.

setup.art: A notebook page with the heading What changed and one large number circled.
setup.caption: 2. Find out what people changed in her place. Write one number as evidence.

setup.art: A poster divided into four boxes with drawings and short notes, held up by a child who is talking to her family.
setup.caption: 3. Make a poster with four boxes. Give a three-minute talk.

flow.do: Help your child choose one animal. Good choices: great Indian bustard, olive ridley turtle, white-rumped vulture, lion-tailed macaque and Nilgiri tahr. Others: gharial, dugong, Indian pangolin, snow leopard and hoolock gibbon. Together, find out where she lives and three of her adaptations. For each adaptation, write the problem it answers.
flow.say: Choose one animal from the list. Where does she live? Find three adaptations. For each one, write the problem it answers: finding food, escaping a hunter, or living with heat, cold or water.
flow.kid: Choose one animal. Find her place. Find three adaptations and the problem each answers.
flow.parent: The websites of WWF-India and the Bombay Natural History Society are good places to start. Sit with your child while they search.
flow.context: This is day 1 of An Animal at Risk. You choose one Indian animal and find the place and three adaptations that fit her to it.

flow.do: Find out what people have changed in her place. Find one number that shows the harm, and write where the number came from. Ask which of her adaptations no longer helps, or now does harm.
flow.say: What did people change in her place? Find one number that shows what happened to her kind. Now look at her three adaptations again. Is there one that does not help against the new danger?
flow.kid: What did people change? Find one number as evidence. Which adaptation fails now?

ask.q: Why can her body not simply change to fit the new danger?
good: Bodies change over many generations.
The place changed in a few years.
Too few are left to have many young.

flow.parent: Examples of a number: only about 100 to 150 great Indian bustards are left. India lost more than 95 of every 100 vultures.
flow.context: This is day 2 of An Animal at Risk. You find out what people changed in the animal's place, with one number as evidence.

flow.do: Your child makes a poster with four boxes: her place, her adaptations, what changed, and what people can do. They can use words, pictures cut from old magazines, or drawings. Then they give a three-minute talk to the family. The family asks two questions.
flow.say: Make your poster with four boxes. Then tell us about her in three minutes. Use your number. Finish with one thing people could do differently.
flow.kid: Make a poster with four boxes. Give a three-minute talk. Use your number.
flow.parent: Listen for the link between the adaptation and the change. A strong talk says why a feature that once helped no longer does.
flow.context: This is day 3 of An Animal at Risk. You make a four-box poster and give a three-minute talk about the animal.

challenges.title: Stand in the Mud: build a mangrove that stays up
challenges.context: In this challenge you build a model tree in a tray of loose rice. The model must stay upright while the tray is shaken. A mangrove tree solves the same problem in soft mud, where the tide pulls twice a day.
challenges.problem: A mangrove tree grows in soft, wet mud. Deep in the mud there is no air, so her roots cannot go far down. Twice a day the tide pushes and pulls at her. Build a model tree that stands in loose rice. The model must stay up when the tray is slid from side to side 10 times.
constraints: The trunk is one pencil with a paper circle 10 centimetres wide taped on top as the crown.
The rice is only 3 centimetres deep.
The trunk may go no more than 2 centimetres into the rice.
You may add up to 8 thin sticks and some tape or thread as roots.
The tree must stay up while the tray is slid 5 centimetres left and right, 10 times.
materials: a tray or a wide vessel with uncooked rice 3 centimetres deep
8 thin sticks, such as broom sticks, toothpicks or used matchsticks
general: Tape sticks to the trunk so that they slope outwards into the rice, like stilts.
Lay sticks flat under the rice, tied to the bottom of the trunk, like a wide foot.
Make the crown smaller, so that there is less weight on top.
creative: Tie three sticks into a tripod halfway up the trunk, so that the tree stands on three legs.
Build two trees side by side and tie their roots together, as mangroves in a forest hold each other.
Use many short roots all the way round in place of a few long ones, and compare.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own roots. Draw the design first, or lay the sticks out as a plan. Test it with 10 slides of the tray, then with 20. Write which roots failed first and what you changed.
