setup.caption: 1. Stand the pencil tree 2 centimetres deep in the rice. Slide the tray. The tree falls.

setup.art: The same pencil tree with four thin sticks taped to the trunk and sloping out into the rice like stilts.
setup.caption: 2. Add roots made of thin sticks.

setup.art: A child sliding the tray from side to side with a ruler beside it, while the pencil tree stays upright.
setup.caption: 3. Slide the tray 5 centimetres left and right, 10 times. Does the tree stay up?

flow.do: Read the problem together. Fill the tray with rice 3 centimetres deep. Stand the bare pencil tree 2 centimetres deep and slide the tray. Ask why it fell and what might hold it up.
flow.say: The tree fell at once. The trunk cannot go deeper, because deep mud has no air for roots. List every idea you have.
flow.kid: Say why the bare tree falls. Then think of ways to hold it up.

ask.q: What could hold a tree up without going deep?
good: Roots that spread wide.
Props that lean out like stilts.
A wide flat foot under the mud.

flow.context: This is the first step of Stand in the Mud. You watch the bare pencil trunk fall, and list ways to keep the model upright.

flow.do: Your child chooses one idea and builds it with up to 8 sticks and some tape or thread.
flow.say: Choose your best idea and build it. Remember the rules: no more than 2 centimetres deep, and no more than 8 sticks.
flow.kid: Build your best idea. Use up to eight sticks.
flow.context: In this step of Stand in the Mud you build roots for the pencil tree from thin sticks.

flow.do: Test it. Slide the tray 5 centimetres left and right, 10 times. Count how many slides the tree survives. Record the number.
flow.say: Now the tide test. Slide the tray left and right ten times, and count aloud. Did the tree stay up?
flow.kid: Slide the tray ten times. Count how many slides the tree survives.
flow.context: In this step of Stand in the Mud you test the rooted pencil tree by sliding the tray 10 times.

flow.do: Change one thing to make it better. Test again. Then look at a picture of a real mangrove with stilt roots, if you can find one, and compare.
flow.say: What failed first? Change one thing and test again. Real mangroves at Pichavaram stand on arching stilt roots. How is your design like theirs, and how is it different?
flow.kid: What failed first? Change one thing. Test again.

ask.q: Why do stilt roots work in soft mud?
good: They spread the tree's weight over a wide area.
They prop the trunk from many sides.
They do not need to go deep.

flow.parent: Praise a clear account of what failed as much as a tree that stays up.
flow.context: This is the last step of Stand in the Mud. You improve your roots and compare them with the stilt roots of a real mangrove.

challenges.title: Shed the Snow, Catch the Sun: design a tree for a snowy hill
challenges.context: In the Snow Load Test experiment earlier in this lesson, a steep paper cone shed almost all the rava snow. A flat paper circle kept all of the rava. In this challenge you design a paper tree that sheds snow and still catches plenty of light.
challenges.problem: A steep cone sheds snow, but it is narrow, so it catches little light from above. A flat tree catches a lot of light and keeps all the snow. Design a paper tree that keeps no more than 2 of 10 teaspoons of rava. The design must also cast the widest shadow you can under a torch.
constraints: Use no more than 2 sheets of paper, and sticky tape.
The tree stands on an upturned tumbler or a bottle, and is no taller than 20 centimetres above it.
Snow test: pour 10 level teaspoons of rava on the top. No more than 2 teaspoons may stay on.
Light test: hold a phone torch 50 centimetres straight above the tree. Measure the width of the shadow on the table.
Do the snow test first. Only a tree that passes may take the light test.
materials: a steel tumbler or a bottle as the trunk
half a cup of dry rava and a teaspoon
general: Make one cone that is steep but as wide at the bottom as the paper allows.
Make a cone with a slope just steep enough for the rava to slide. Find that slope by testing.
Use smooth, shiny paper, so that the rava slides at a gentler slope.
creative: Stack three or four small sloping skirts down the trunk, like the layers of branches on a real deodar.
Make branches from paper strips that bend down under a load and spring back when it slides off.
Give each branch a narrow tip that points down, so that the rava runs off the end.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own tree. Plan it first: draw it, or tell your grown-up the plan. Run the snow test and then the light test. Write the two numbers, change one thing, and test again.

setup.art: A narrow steep paper cone beside a wide flat paper circle, each on an upturned tumbler, with a small heap of rava on the flat one.
setup.caption: 1. A steep cone sheds snow and catches little light. A flat tree does the opposite.

setup.art: A paper tree made of three sloping paper skirts stacked down a bottle, with rava sliding off each layer.
setup.caption: 2. Design a tree that sheds the snow. Pour 10 teaspoons of rava on top.

setup.art: A hand holding a phone torch above the layered paper tree, with a ruler measuring the round shadow on the table.
setup.caption: 3. Hold a torch 50 centimetres above. Measure the width of the shadow.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Remind your child of the Snow Load Test. There the steep cone shed almost all the rava, and the flat circle kept all of the rava. Ask what a tree needs light for, and list design ideas.
flow.say: In the Snow Load Test the steep cone shed the snow, but it was narrow. A tree makes food with light, so a narrow tree makes less food. List every idea you have.
flow.kid: Why does a narrow tree make less food?

ask.q: How could a tree be wide and still shed snow?
good: Many small slopes in layers.
Branches that bend down when loaded.
A slope that is only just steep enough.

flow.context: This is the first step of Shed the Snow, Catch the Sun. You list ways for one paper tree to shed rava snow and still catch light.

flow.do: Your child chooses one idea and builds it from no more than 2 sheets of paper. Stand it on the tumbler or bottle.
flow.say: Choose your best idea and build it. Keep it under 20 centimetres tall. Think about where the rava will go when it slides.
flow.kid: Build your best idea from two sheets. Keep it under 20 centimetres.
flow.context: In this step of Shed the Snow, Catch the Sun you build your paper tree.

flow.do: Run the snow test: pour 10 level teaspoons of rava on the top and measure what stays on. If 2 teaspoons or fewer stay, run the light test. Hold the torch 50 centimetres above and measure the width of the shadow. Record both numbers.
flow.say: Snow test first. Ten teaspoons on the top. How many stayed on? If it is two or fewer, we do the light test. How wide is the shadow?
flow.kid: Pour ten teaspoons. Count what stays. Then measure the shadow.
flow.context: In this step of Shed the Snow, Catch the Sun you test how much rava your design keeps. Then you measure the shadow.

flow.do: Change one thing and test again. Then talk about the question below.
flow.say: Which number do you want to improve? Change one thing and test again. A real deodar has layers of sloping branches. What does that design gain?
flow.kid: Change one thing. Test again. Did the other number get worse?

ask.q: Why can a tree not be best at shedding snow and best at catching light?
good: A steep shape is narrow.
A wide shape gives snow a place to sit.
Making one better makes the other worse.

flow.parent: The wider the shadow, the more light the tree would catch. Most designs gain on one test and lose on the other. Layers of sloping branches do well on both.
flow.context: This is the last step of Shed the Snow, Catch the Sun. You improve your paper tree and see how one test trades against the other.

items.p: What is an adaptation?
opts: An inherited feature that helps survival
A skill an animal learns by practice
A place where an animal lives
items.why: An adaptation is inherited from parents and helps a living thing survive and have young in their place. A learned skill is not inherited.

items.p: Why are a tiger's eyes at the front of her face?
opts: To judge the distance to her prey
items.why: Both eyes see the same deer from slightly different places. The brain uses the two views to judge the distance. A hunter needs that to leap exactly.

items.p: Which of these is a behavioural adaptation?
opts: A lizard resting in a burrow at noon
items.why: A behavioural adaptation is something a living thing does. Wide feet, spines and a thick coat are parts of the body, so they are structural adaptations.

items.p: Bright colours that tell hunters an animal is bitter or can sting are called ____ colours.
items.why: Warning colours are easy to see and easy to remember. A hunter who has had one bad meal avoids the pattern afterwards.

items.p: The animal who is copied is the model. The animal who copies her look is the ____.
items.why: A mimic gains from looking like the model. The female danaid eggfly is a mimic of the bitter plain tiger.

items.p: A porcupine can shoot her quills at an attacker.
items.why: False. The quills are loosely fixed in her skin. She runs backwards into the attacker, and the quills come off when they touch.

items.p: Camouflage is used by hunters as well as by prey.
items.why: True. A tiger's stripes and a crab spider's colour help them to get close to prey without being noticed.

items.p: Match each plant to the place she is adapted to.
pairs: A cactus with spines and a thick stem
A lotus with air tubes in her stems
Soft, salty mud by the sea
items.why: Each feature answers a problem of the place. Spines save water, and air tubes carry oxygen to roots in mud. Stilt roots hold a tree up in soft ground, and sloping branches shed snow.

items.p: Sort these adaptations. Does each one help a predator, or help prey?
items: eyes at the front of the face
eyes at the sides of the head
items.why: Ask what problem each one solves. Fangs, silent wings and forward eyes help to catch. Side eyes, a tail that breaks off and armour help against being caught.

items.p: Put a tiger's hunt in order, from her first problem to her last.
items: Find a deer by sight, sound or smell
a: Find a deer by sight, sound or smell
items.why: A hunter must find prey before she can get near, and get near before she can catch and kill. Each step has adaptations of its own.

items.p: Why does snow slide off a steep, cone-shaped tree?
opts: Snow cannot grip so steep a slope
The needles push the snow away
items.why: On a steep slope, the weight of the snow drags it downhill more strongly than the surface can hold it. In the Snow Load Test, rava slides off a steep paper cone in the same way.

items.p: A hoverfly has no sting, but she is striped like a wasp. What is this called?
items.why: Mimicry is one kind of animal looking like another kind and gaining from it. Birds who have been stung by a wasp leave the hoverfly alone.

items.p: Explain in two sentences why a plain tiger butterfly gains by being easy to see.
items.a: She tastes bitter. A bird who has tried one remembers the bright colours and leaves the others alone. If she were hidden, birds would not learn to avoid her kind.
items.why: A strong answer says that she has a real defence, and that the bright colour helps hunters to remember it.

items.p: A camel and a spiny-tailed lizard both live in desert heat. Describe how each one deals with it.
items.a: The camel stays out in the heat. Her body can warm up by about 6 degrees without harm, so she sweats little. The lizard avoids the heat by resting in her burrow in the hottest hours.
items.why: A strong answer shows two different answers to one problem: one animal puts up with the heat, and the other avoids it.

items.p: Draw a hunter's head and a prey animal's head from the front. Show the eyes.
items.a: The hunter's head, such as a cat's, has both eyes at the front. The prey's head, such as a goat's or a deer's, has one eye on each side.
items.why: A strong drawing puts the hunter's eyes side by side, facing forward. The prey's eyes are far apart, on the sides of the head.
items.art: A blank box with two faint outline circles, one labelled hunter and one labelled prey.

worksheets.title: Fitting a place, and fitting each other

items.p: A deer's eyes have two kinds of colour cells. How does a tiger's orange coat look to her?
opts: Much like the green of grass
items.why: With two kinds of colour cells, a deer does not tell orange from green well. So the coat that looks bright to us blends with the grass for a deer.

items.p: Which kind of camouflage does a stick insect use?
opts: Masquerade: she looks like a twig
items.why: In masquerade the animal can be seen, but she looks like something not worth eating. A bird sees a twig and moves on.

items.p: A chilli burns a rat's mouth and has no effect on a bird's. How does this help the chilli plant?
opts: The burn makes the seeds grow
items.why: Rats crush the seeds with their teeth, and the burn keeps them away. Birds swallow the seeds whole and drop them somewhere new.

items.p: Why do many leaves in rainy forests end in a long, narrow tip?
opts: Rain runs to the tip and drips off
items.why: A leaf that stays wet catches less light, and moulds grow on it. A drip tip helps the leaf to dry sooner.

items.p: A chameleon's biggest colour changes are signals to other chameleons.
items.why: True. Scientists who studied dwarf chameleons found the biggest and fastest changes during displays to rivals and mates. Hiding is only part of the story.

items.p: In the common mormon butterfly, both males and females are mimics.
items.why: False. Only some of the females copy the poisonous common rose. The males, and the other females, are black with a row of white spots.

items.p: Sort these adaptations into three kinds.
items: a gecko hunting near a light at night
a camel's body warming by 6 degrees
a seabird's body passing out extra salt
items.why: A structural adaptation is a part of the body. A behavioural one is an action. A physiological one is a way the body works inside.

items.p: Three of these animals use warning colours. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: The butterfly, the wasp and the krait gain by being noticed. A nightjar gains by not being noticed, which is camouflage.

items.p: A herd has 20 deer. Each hunt takes 1 at random. How many of 100 hunts take one chosen deer?
items.why: About 5. Each deer has 1 chance in 20, and one twentieth of 100 is 5. Alone, she would be the target in all 100 hunts.

items.p: Match each model to her mimic.
items.why: Each model has a real defence: bitter taste, a sting or venom. Each mimic is harmless and looks like her model.

items.p: In the Copycat Test, a hunter eats few striped squares and many dotted ones. Explain why.
items.a: Most striped squares were bitter, so the hunter lost points and learned to avoid stripes. Most dotted squares were tasty, so the hunter learned that dots were safe and kept eating.
items.why: A strong answer says that the hunter judges a pattern by the meals it has given so far.

items.p: A great Indian bustard has eyes on the sides of her head. How does this help her, and harm her?
items.a: Side-facing eyes let her watch the ground and the sky all round for foxes and eagles. But she sees poorly straight ahead when she flies, so she does not see power lines in time.
items.why: A strong answer shows that the same feature helps against the old danger and fails against the new one.

items.p: Many people think bright colours in nature always mean danger. Give one example that fits and one that does not.
items.a: It fits a wasp, whose yellow and black warn of a sting. It does not fit a ripe mango, whose colour invites animals to eat the fruit and carry the seed.
items.why: A strong answer shows that a colour is a signal. The meaning depends on who is sending the signal and why.

items.p: Power lines cross the grassland where the last great Indian bustards live. People are deciding what to do.

views.says: Bustards see poorly straight ahead when they fly, and fewer than 150 are left. The lines in their grassland should go underground.
These lines carry clean power to millions of homes. Burying them costs many times more. Hang shining flaps on the wires.

views.who: A herder from a nearby village
views.says: We have grazed sheep beside these birds for generations. Ask us where the birds fly, and bury only those stretches.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason, using what you know about the bustard's eyes. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason from the unit. One reason is that side-facing eyes do not show the bird a wire ahead. Another is that flaps make the wire easier to see from the side.
items.why: Each view has something right in it. A strong answer uses the bustard's field of view, and takes the cost and the local knowledge seriously.

items.p: Draw a cactus. Then label three adaptations, and write what each one does.
a: Spines: they lose far less water than leaves, and keep grazing animals away
Waxy skin: it slows the escape of water
items.why: A strong answer links each part to the problem of a dry place: little water, and animals who want it.
items.art: A blank box for the child's own drawing of a cactus, with three empty label lines beside it.

items.p: Jays who had never met a monarch butterfly ate the look-alike viceroy. What does this show?
opts: A mimic is protected only by experienced hunters
items.why: The pattern meant nothing to jays who had never had a bad meal from it. Only jays who had tasted a monarch refused the viceroy.

items.p: Factory smoke blackened the tree trunks. Why did pale peppered moths become rare?
opts: Birds found them easily on dark bark
Each moth turned dark in the soot
They flew away to the cities
items.why: Pale wings no longer matched the trunks, so birds ate most pale moths. Dark moths were born dark. No moth changed colour in her own lifetime.

items.p: Two bitter kinds of butterfly share one wing pattern. How does each kind gain?
opts: Hunters need to learn only one pattern
items.why: Some butterflies die while young birds are learning. If two bitter kinds share a pattern, they share those losses.

items.p: Collars on cheetahs and impalas recorded their chases. How did impalas usually escape?
opts: By turning sharply at a lower speed
By running faster than the cheetah
items.why: The cheetahs were faster. A fast body needs more room to turn, so a sharp turn at the last moment made the cheetah overshoot.

items.p: Over many generations, hunters and their prey change each other.
items.why: True. Prey who notice or escape a little better have more young, and so do hunters who catch a little better. This is co-evolution.

items.p: Ten bitter squares score minus 2 each. Two tasty squares score plus 1 each. How many points are lost overall?
items.why: The bitter squares lose 10 times 2, which is 20 points. The tasty squares win 2 points. 20 minus 2 is 18 points lost. Eating striped squares in the first hunt of the Copycat Test does not pay.

items.p: A paper tree keeps 4 of the 10 teaspoons of rava poured on it. What percentage slides off?
items.why: 10 minus 4 is 6 teaspoons that slide off. 6 out of 10 is 60 out of 100, which is 60 per cent.

items.p: Two kinds of living things changing over many generations, each because of the other, is called ____.
items.why: Bats and moths have shaped each other in this way. So have cheetahs and antelopes, and milkweed and the plain tiger caterpillar.

items.p: Put these events in order, to show how peppered moths changed near Manchester.
items: Pale moths rest unseen on pale, lichen-covered trunks
Factory smoke kills the lichen and blackens the trunks
Birds find and eat most of the pale moths
Dark moths survive and have more young
Almost all the moths in the area are dark
a: Pale moths rest unseen on pale, lichen-covered trunks
Factory smoke kills the lichen and blackens the trunks
Birds find and eat most of the pale moths
Dark moths survive and have more young
Almost all the moths in the area are dark
items.why: The place changed first. Then the birds' hunting changed which moths lived, and the dark form spread over many generations.

items.p: The steep cone in the Snow Load Test is narrower than the flat tree. Why is the test still fair?
items.a: All the rava is poured on the very top of each tree, so every tree receives the same 10 teaspoons. The paper, the circle size and the pouring height are also the same.
items.why: A strong answer notices that width could matter, and then shows how pouring on the tip removes that difference.

items.p: Design a test: do birds near your home avoid yellow and black food? Say what you would keep the same.
items.a: For example: put out ten plain rice balls and ten rice balls striped with haldi and black sesame. Use the same size, the same place and the same time each day. Count how many of each are eaten over five days, and swap their positions each day.
items.why: A strong answer changes only the colour, keeps size, place and time the same, repeats the test, and counts.

items.p: Only female common mormon butterflies are mimics. Suggest one reason, and say how you could test it.
items.a: Nobody knows for certain. One idea is that a female carrying eggs flies slowly and needs more protection. Another is that males need their own pattern so that females recognise them. A test could compare how often birds attack paper models of each pattern.
items.why: This is an open question. A strong answer gives a reason that could be true and a test that could show it to be wrong.

items.p: A village beside a forest keeps losing goats to a leopard at night. People are deciding what to do.

views.says: Each goat is a month's income for my family. The leopard should be caught and moved far away.
A leopard who is moved often walks back, or another leopard takes the empty place. Strong night sheds protect goats better.
A leopard is fitted to hunting by stealth in the dark. Lights and closed sheds take away exactly what her adaptations need.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason, using what you know about predator adaptations. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason from the unit. One reason is that a leopard's camouflage and night vision work only when she can get close unseen. Another is that the owner's loss is real and must be met.
items.why: Each view has something right in it. A strong answer uses the leopard's adaptations, and takes the family's loss seriously.

items.p: Invent a prey animal for a snowy mountain where one hunter lives. Draw her, and label three adaptations.
items.a: For example: a hare-like animal with a white winter coat for camouflage and wide furry feet for soft snow. Her eyes are on the sides of the head, to watch for the hunter.
items.why: A strong drawing has one adaptation for the cold or the snow, and one against the hunter. Each has a reason.
items.art: A blank box with a small corner sketch of a snowy slope and rocks.

items.p: Match each kind of camouflage to its example.
pairs: A tiger's stripes in tall grass
A fish with a dark back and a pale belly
A butterfly who looks like a dead leaf
items.why: Matching blends with the background. A disruptive pattern breaks the outline. Countershading cancels the belly's shadow. Masquerade makes the animal look like some other thing.

quiz.p: Which of these is an adaptation?
quiz.why: An adaptation is inherited and helps a living thing survive in their place. Learning to sit is learned, and a scar is not passed on to young.

quiz.p: Which of these is a physiological adaptation?
opts: A cactus opening her skin holes at night
quiz.why: A physiological adaptation is a way the body works inside. Claws and shape are structural, and living in herds is behavioural.

quiz.p: A tree lives in soft, salty mud where the tide pulls. Which adaptation suits her?
quiz.why: Stilt roots prop a mangrove from many sides in soft mud. A deep root would find no air in the mud. Needles and a cone shape suit snow.

quiz.p: Why does a yak have a thick double coat?
opts: To hold her body heat in the cold
quiz.why: The coat traps a layer of air, and trapped air lets little heat through. In the cold of Ladakh that saves her energy.

quiz.p: Why do many prey animals have eyes on the sides of the head?
opts: To see almost all the way round
quiz.why: Side-facing eyes give a wide field of view, so a hunter is noticed from almost any direction. Judging distance exactly needs two eyes on the same thing, as a hunter has.

quiz.p: What does living in a herd give each deer?
opts: A smaller share of the risk
quiz.why: A hunter takes one animal, and in a herd each deer is one among many. Many eyes also notice the hunter sooner.

quiz.p: A tiger's stripes break up her outline. What is this kind of camouflage called?
quiz.why: A disruptive pattern cuts the body's shape into pieces, so the watcher does not see one animal. Masquerade is looking like some other thing, such as a twig.

quiz.p: Why does a bitter butterfly gain from bright colours?
opts: Birds remember her and avoid her kind
quiz.why: A bold pattern is easy to notice and remember. A bird who has had one bad meal then leaves that pattern alone. The poison is in her body, not in the colour.

quiz.p: When is a harmless mimic safest?
quiz.why: Hunters avoid a pattern that usually gives a bad meal. If mimics outnumber models, or the models vanish, hunters learn that the pattern is safe to eat.

quiz.p: In a fair test of paper tree shapes, what should be the only thing that changes?
quiz.why: A fair test changes one thing and keeps the rest the same. Then any difference in the result must come from the slope.

quiz.p: Why do great Indian bustards die on power lines?
opts: They see poorly straight ahead in flight
They like to sit on wires
quiz.why: Their eyes are on the sides of the head, which suits watching for foxes and eagles. Wires straight ahead are a new danger that those eyes do not show in time.

applications: Road signs, safety vests and danger labels use red, yellow and black, the same warning colours that wasps use. They can be seen from far away and are easy to remember.
Soldiers' uniforms and bird-watchers' hides use camouflage patterns that break up the outline, as a tiger's stripes do.
In Rajasthan, people hang shining flaps called bird diverters on power lines. The flaps help great Indian bustards to see the wires.
Farmers in Botswana painted eyes on the rumps of cattle. Lions hunt by ambush, and during the four-year study no painted cow was killed.
In the Sundarbans in the 1980s, honey collectors wore face masks on the back of the head. Tigers are said to attack from behind.
Farmers in Assam hang ropes smeared with chilli around fields. The burning chemical that protects the chilli plant also turns elephants away.
Houses in Himachal Pradesh and Kashmir have steep sloping roofs. Snow slides off before the weight can break the roof.

open_questions.q: Why are only female common mormon butterflies mimics?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have found the gene that switches the pattern on. They have several ideas about why males never use it, and no test has settled the matter.

open_questions.q: What are a zebra's stripes for?
open_questions.why_open: The best evidence says the stripes keep biting flies from landing. But scientists still argue about cooling and about dazzling a hunter.

open_questions.q: How does a plant tell a caterpillar's chewing from the shaking of the wind?
open_questions.why_open: Cress plants raise their defences after feeling the vibrations of chewing, and not after wind or insect song. Nobody yet knows how the plant tells them apart.

open_questions.q: Why do some poisonous animals stay hidden while others advertise?
open_questions.why_open: Some poisonous toads and caterpillars are dull and camouflaged. Scientists have several ideas about when a warning pays, and the evidence is mixed.

open_questions.q: How fast can living things adapt to places that people are changing?
open_questions.why_open: Peppered moths changed within about fifty years. Large animals with few young, such as bustards, may not have that much time. Nobody can predict which kinds will keep up.

maths.problem: In the Snow Load Test, 10 teaspoons of rava were poured on each paper tree. The flat tree kept 10, the low cone kept 5 and the steep cone kept 1. What percentage of the rava slid off each tree?
maths.answer: Flat tree: 0 per cent. Low cone: 50 per cent. Steep cone: 90 per cent.
maths.explain: Take away what stayed on from 10. The flat tree lost 0, the low cone lost 5 and the steep cone lost 9. Out of 10, these are 0 tenths, 5 tenths and 9 tenths. As percentages they are 0, 50 and 90.
maths.context: In the Snow Load Test you pour rava on a flat paper tree, a low cone and a steep cone. You measure how much stays on. These are made-up results.

chart.title: Made-up example: teaspoons of rava that stayed on, out of 10

maths.why_maths: A percentage lets you compare trees even if you pour a different amount next time.

maths.problem: In the Snow Load Test, each paper circle is folded into 8 equal slices. What is the angle of one slice at the centre? The steep cone has 4 slices tucked under. How many degrees of paper are left showing?
maths.answer: One slice is 45 degrees. The steep cone shows 180 degrees, which is half the circle.
maths.explain: A full turn is 360 degrees. 360 divided by 8 is 45. Four slices are 4 times 45, which is 180 degrees tucked under. 360 minus 180 leaves 180 degrees showing.
maths.context: In the Snow Load Test you fold a paper circle in half three times to mark 8 slices. Tucking slices under turns the circle into a cone.
maths.why_maths: The more degrees you tuck under, the steeper the cone. Angles let you say exactly how each tree was made, so that someone else can repeat the test.

maths.problem: In the Copycat Test a tasty square scores plus 1 and a bitter square scores minus 2. Hunt 1 has 12 striped squares: 10 bitter and 2 tasty. Hunt 2 has 12 dotted squares: 2 bitter and 10 tasty. What would a hunter score for eating all 12 patterned squares in each hunt?
maths.explain: Hunt 1: 10 bitter squares lose 20 points and 2 tasty squares win 2, which makes minus 18. Hunt 2: 2 bitter squares lose 4 points and 10 tasty squares win 10, which makes plus 6. So eating the pattern pays only in hunt 2.
maths.context: In the Copycat Test a hunter turns over paper squares. Some patterned squares are bitter, and some are harmless copycats.
maths.why_maths: The totals show why a sensible hunter avoids stripes in hunt 1 and eats dots in hunt 2. Both patterns hide copycats.

maths.problem: A hunter faces 12 patterned squares, with plus 1 for tasty and minus 2 for bitter. How many of the 12 must be bitter before eating all of them scores 0 or less?
maths.answer: 4 or more. With 4 bitter and 8 tasty, the score is exactly 0.
maths.explain: Try the numbers in order. With 3 bitter and 9 tasty, the score is 9 minus 6, which is plus 3. With 4 bitter and 8 tasty, it is 8 minus 8, which is 0. With 5 bitter it is 7 minus 10, which is minus 3. So the pattern stops paying when one third of the squares are bitter.
maths.context: In the Copycat Test, harmless copycats are safe only if a hunter gives up on their pattern. This problem finds the point where the hunter should give up.
maths.why_maths: Finding the balance point tells you how many harmful models a pattern needs before copycats are protected. A nastier model would need fewer.

maths.problem: In Edge or Middle, the herd has 19 chana. There are 12 on the edge, 6 in the inner ring and 1 in the centre. The marble tiger attacked 12 times and caught an edge chana every time. What fraction of the herd was never in danger? If a deer stood alone, how many of 12 attacks would be aimed at her?
maths.answer: 7 of the 19 were never in danger. A deer alone is the target of all 12 attacks.
maths.explain: The inner ring and the centre make 6 plus 1, which is 7 chana out of 19. The 12 attacks were shared among the 12 edge chana, about 1 each. A deer alone has nobody to share with, so all 12 attacks are hers.
maths.context: In Edge or Middle, 19 chana stand in three rings as a herd, and a rolling marble is the tiger. The first chana touched is caught.
maths.why_maths: Counting each animal's share of the attacks turns 'a herd is safer' into numbers you can compare.

maths.problem: A cheetah runs 28 metres each second, and a blackbuck runs 22 metres each second. The blackbuck starts 60 metres ahead and runs straight. How long does the cheetah take to catch up? A cheetah can sprint for about 20 seconds. Does she catch the blackbuck?
maths.answer: 10 seconds. Yes, if the blackbuck runs straight.
maths.explain: Each second the cheetah gains 28 minus 22, which is 6 metres. 60 divided by 6 is 10 seconds. That is less than 20 seconds, so the cheetah catches up. This is why a blackbuck swerves, as the runner does in Turn or Sprint.
maths.context: In Turn or Sprint a faster chaser tries to tag a slower runner. This problem works out a straight chase between a cheetah and a blackbuck, with round numbers.
maths.why_maths: The gap closes by the difference between the two speeds. Working it out shows that speed alone cannot save the slower animal.

Warning colours make an animal easy to see.
A bitter or stinging animal gains when hunters notice and remember her.
A hoverfly can sting like a wasp.

A porcupine can shoot her quills.

A cactus's spines lose less water than leaves would.

Snow slides off a steep cone more easily than off a flat top.
On a steep slope the weight of the snow drags it downhill.
A deer in a herd is in more danger than a deer alone.

The cactus, the camel and the lizard are adapted to dry places, but a lotus lives in a pond.
The hoverfly, the eggfly and the wolf snake are harmless mimics, but the common rose is a poisonous model.
Paws, fur and webbed feet are parts of the body, but living in a herd is a behaviour.

how_we_found_out.context: This card tells how people found out what bright colours and look-alike wings are for.
how_we_found_out.story: Henry Walter Bates spent eleven years in the Amazon forest. In 1862 he wrote about a puzzle. Some butterflies from quite different families had almost the same wings. Some naturalists said the same forest and climate had coloured them alike. Bates suggested that harmless kinds were copying kinds that birds avoid. In 1867 Charles Darwin had a puzzle of his own. He thought bright colours helped animals to win mates. But many caterpillars are bright, and caterpillars do not mate. He asked Alfred Russel Wallace. Wallace guessed that bright caterpillars taste bad, and that the colour helps birds to remember them. John Jenner Weir tested this in his aviary and reported in 1869. His birds ate dull caterpillars and refused bright ones. Nobody tested the copying itself with live birds until the 1950s. Jane Van Zandt Brower fed bitter monarch butterflies to Florida scrub jays. Jays who had tried a monarch then refused viceroy butterflies, which look like monarchs. Jays who had never met a monarch ate the viceroys.
how_we_found_out.who: Henry Walter Bates, Charles Darwin, Alfred Russel Wallace and John Jenner Weir in England, and Jane Van Zandt Brower in the United States
how_we_found_out.when: Bates wrote in 1862. Darwin and Wallace exchanged letters in 1867, and Weir reported his tests in 1869. Jane Brower published her jay tests in 1958.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That look-alike butterflies were coloured alike by their surroundings, and that bright colours were only for winning mates. Weir's birds showed that bright colours can be warnings. Brower's jays showed that a copy protects only against birds who have met the bitter kind.
how_we_found_out.art: A woman scientist in the 1950s holding an orange and black butterfly in tweezers in front of a cage with a blue and grey jay, who is turning her head away.

roots.context: In this lesson you poured rava snow on paper trees and hunted paper prey with false warnings. Here we ask a bigger question. Does a warning pattern belong only to the animal who carries the pattern, or does the protection also depend on other living beings?

deep_truth.truth: In the first hunt of the Copycat Test, most striped squares were bitter, so the hunter left the harmless striped squares alone too. In the second hunt, most dotted squares were harmless, so the hunter ate them. A copied warning works only while hunters keep meeting the real, bitter kind. So one animal's safety can depend on the bodies of other animals.
deep_truth.habit: We talk about an adaptation as something an animal owns, like a tool in a bag. But the copied pattern worked in one hunt and failed in the other. The copycat did not change. What changed was how many bitter squares were on the table around it.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Copycat Test only the share of copycats changed, from 2 in 12 to 10 in 12. Jane Brower's jays refused viceroy butterflies only after they had tasted monarchs. David Pfennig's team put out clay copies of a harmless banded snake. In places with no coral snakes, the copies were attacked more often.

three.who_am_i: You depend on shared warnings too. A red traffic light keeps you safe only while most drivers stop at red.
three.what_is_life: No living being is adapted alone. A deer's speed answers the tiger, and a tiger's stripes answer the deer's eyes.
three.what_is_this_world: A place is more than rock, water and weather. The other living beings are part of every place.

roots.thread: A camel is suited to sand, and a deodar is suited to snow. A mimic butterfly is suited to something you cannot see, which is a bird's memory of a bad meal. That memory exists only because another butterfly is bitter. So one wing pattern ties three living beings together. Nagarjuna taught that each thing is what it is through other things. Mimicry is a clear case that science can test.

teachings.source: Nagarjuna, Mulamadhyamakakarika 24.18 to 24.19 (about the 2nd century CE)
teachings.teaching: Nagarjuna taught that nothing has its nature all by itself. Whatever exists has arisen in dependence on other things.
teachings.link: Nagarjuna was writing about all things, and he did not mention butterflies. A warning pattern is a small case that fits. Orange and black have no power by themselves. Their power comes from a poison in one body and a memory in another.

teachings.source: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1859), the last paragraph
teachings.teaching: Darwin asks the reader to look at a tangled river bank with many plants, singing birds, insects and worms. He says these living forms are very different from each other, and depend on each other in complex ways.
teachings.link: Darwin wrote this three years before Bates described mimicry. Mimicry became one of the clearest examples of what he meant. A mimic's wings cannot be explained without the model and the bird.

science.text: Many moths have ears that hear the calls of hunting bats. The barbastelle bat calls very softly, and catches moths who would hear a louder bat. Each body has been shaped by the other.
In the common mormon butterfly only females are mimics. Scientists have found the gene that switches the pattern on, but they still argue about why males never use it.

other_view.who: Many biologists who follow the gene's-eye view that Richard Dawkins set out in The Selfish Gene (1976)
other_view.view: The mimic and the model are not partners. The mimic gains, and the model loses a little whenever a bird is fooled into trying the pattern again. On this view each body is built by genes that helped their own carriers. The ties between living things are real, but they are mostly ties of use and conflict.

practice.title: One minute at the window: what problem does each part of this body solve?
practice.say: Stand at a window and choose one living being, such as a crow, a tree or an ant. Look at her quietly for one minute. For each part of her body, ask what problem outside her body it solves. The wing solves the problem of moving through air. The beak solves the problem of picking up a seed or a scrap. The watchful eye solves the problem of spotting a cat. Now look at your own hand, and ask the same question.
practice.kid: Stand at a window. Choose one living being. Look quietly for one minute. What problem does each body part solve? Now ask the same about your hand.

playtest: Read through as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, step by step. The experiments were reasoned through carefully but not yet tried at home. The Snow Load Test (core) needs three sheets of stiff paper, a small plate to draw round and tape. It also needs a tumbler, a tray and half a cup of dry rava. The flat tree should keep nearly all 10 teaspoons and the steep cone almost none. The low cone varies with the paper: on shiny paper most of the rava slides off, and on rough paper a heap stays. Thin paper sags, so the step says to tape two sheets together. Damp salt clumps, so rava is the first choice. The Copycat Test (core) needs two sheets of notebook paper, a crayon and a pencil. A grown-up must make the 32 squares in secret, which takes about seven minutes. Most hunters stop eating striped squares after one to three bitter ones. They eat most dotted squares in the second hunt. A very careful hunter may stop early in both hunts, and the step tells the parent what to say then. The letters must be small and in pencil, and the squares must lie on newspaper so that nothing shows through. Edge or Middle needs chana placed a finger-width apart. If the gaps are wider than the marble, the marble can pass the outer ring, so keep them narrow. Bitter Leaf, Sweet Fruit uses only kitchen foods, and a grown-up cuts them. Turn or Sprint needs a clear space of about 15 big steps and is marked as optional. Stand in the Mud needs a tray of rice 3 centimetres deep, which can be cooked afterwards. Shed the Snow, Catch the Sun needs a phone torch and a dim room, so that the shadow is clear. Bitter or Bluff needs two players, and the truth rule must be read aloud before play. An Animal at Risk needs a grown-up beside the child for the searching. No part needs a garden, a pet or a wild animal.
